items.title: Exposed Debug/Backdoor Functionality
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A disassembler/decompiler appropriate to the runtime (dnSpy/ILSpy for .NET, Ghidra/IDA for native binaries, jadx for JVM-based clients). Standard (non-administrative) user access is sufficient for most discovery steps.
items.whatItIs: Debug consoles, hidden developer menus, or hardcoded 'master' passwords that were built in to help developers test the app, but never got removed before the app shipped to customers. They might be triggered by a secret hotkey, an undocumented command-line switch, or a hidden menu — but once someone finds the trigger, they get access to functionality regular users were never meant to have.
items.rootCause: This kind of debug code usually gets left in and just 'hidden' behind an obscure trigger, instead of actually being deleted or stripped out of the release build. There's no automated check in the build process to catch these leftovers before the software ships.
items.impact: What this exposes decides the severity. At the lower end it leaks internal state and unmasked configuration. At the upper end it becomes a full authentication bypass or arbitrary code execution, where the debug path allows loading unsigned plugins, disabling licence checks, or running commands with the application's own privileges.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the binary and search for suspicious string literals: "debug", "backdoor", "master", "test mode", "godmode", hardcoded hotkey combinations, or hidden command-line flag names.

Enumerate all command-line switches the binary recognizes (via decompiled argument-parsing logic) rather than relying only on the documented `--help` output, since undocumented flags are the whole point of this finding.
Check application configuration files and the registry/plist for undocumented keys that toggle debug/diagnostic behavior when present.

Fuzz common debug-trigger patterns (Ctrl+Shift+D style hotkey combinations, triple-click sequences, specific menu-click orders) while monitoring the application's window/log output for unexpected UI changes.
Review any embedded update/telemetry channel for a debug or staging environment flag that, if left toggleable client-side, might reconnect the shipped client to a less-hardened backend.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes reverse engineering and use of any discovered debug/backdoor functionality against the test installation.
Trigger the discovered debug interface (hotkey, CLI flag, hidden menu) and document exactly what functionality it exposes.

If the debug path exposes elevated actions (bypassing license checks, unlocking admin-only features, disabling certificate validation, or providing a script/command console), demonstrate the resulting impact using benign, non-destructive test actions only.
Where a hardcoded backdoor credential or master password is found, confirm it authenticates successfully against a test account/instance and document the exact value and its scope of access.
Check whether the same binary/build is distributed to all customers (making the backdoor a universal, not per-deployment, risk) versus being unique per license.

examplePayloads.label: Search decompiled strings for debug/backdoor indicators
.NET decompilation for hidden logic
examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app.exe  # inspect for conditional branches gated on hardcoded strings/env vars

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate all recognized CLI switches from decompiled arg-parsing
Test discovered debug flag

variants: Hardcoded master/support password that bypasses normal authentication entirely, often left in place to ease vendor support calls.
Undocumented environment variable (e.g. APP_DEBUG=1) that disables license/certificate checks when set.
Hidden menu item revealed only via an unusual UI interaction sequence, exposing internal diagnostic or admin functionality.
mitigation: Strip all debug/diagnostic code paths from release builds via conditional compilation (#if DEBUG or equivalent), not just UI-level hiding.
Add a release-pipeline check (static analysis rule) that fails the build if known debug-trigger strings or hardcoded credentials are present in the compiled binary.
Never ship hardcoded master passwords or support backdoors; use a properly authenticated, audited, time-limited remote-support mechanism instead.
Conduct a pre-release binary audit (string extraction, decompilation spot-check) as a standing release gate for thick-client software.

items.title: Insecure Registry Key Permissions Storing Configuration
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access. Registry inspection tools (regedit, accesschk from Sysinternals) on Windows, or equivalent file-permission inspection tools for the plist/config-file storage location on macOS/Linux clients.
items.whatItIs: The app stores its settings — which might include connection details, feature flags, license info, or references to credentials — in a Windows registry key. That key's permissions allow regular, non-admin users (or even 'Everyone') to write to it, instead of restricting writes to administrators only.
items.rootCause: The installer either just inherits permissions from the parent registry key, or deliberately grants broad write access to avoid annoying admin-permission popups when the app needs to save a setting. It doesn't account for the fact that any other program running as that same user — including malware — can write to the exact same location.
items.impact: A local low-privileged attacker, or malware running as an ordinary user, can edit the application's configuration. That lets them point the client at a server they control, or switch off security features such as certificate validation and update signature checks wherever those are configuration-driven. They can also plant a value that gets loaded later by a higher-privileged companion service, which turns a user-level write into privileged execution.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the application's registry footprint (typically under HKLM\SOFTWARE\<Vendor>\<App> for machine-wide settings) using Process Monitor to capture actual reads/writes during normal operation.
Run accesschk against every discovered key to enumerate effective permissions for the Users/Authenticated Users/Everyone groups.

Flag any key writable by non-administrators that is also read by a higher-privileged component (an auto-start service, a scheduled task running as SYSTEM) as the highest-severity variant of this finding.

Cross-reference writable keys against what configuration they actually control (feature flags vs. security-relevant settings like certificate pinning toggles or server endpoints) to correctly scope severity.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes registry-permission testing and modification against the local test installation.
As a standard user, attempt to write a test value to each flagged key and confirm the write succeeds without an access-denied error.

If a security-relevant setting is writable (e.g. a server endpoint URL, a disable-certificate-validation flag), modify it to point at a benign, attacker-controlled test endpoint and confirm the running application picks up the change.

If a privileged component (SYSTEM service) reads the same key, demonstrate escalation by writing a value that causes that component to execute or load attacker-supplied content, then trigger the privileged component to run.
Restore the original registry values after the proof-of-concept and document the exact key path, current DACL, and recommended fix.

examplePayloads.label: Capture actual registry reads/writes during normal use
examplePayloads.command: procmon.exe /AcceptEula /Quiet /BackingFile capture.pml  # filter on Path contains <VendorName> after capture

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate effective permissions on a discovered key
Test standard-user write access directly

variants: Writable HKLM key read by an auto-start SYSTEM service, enabling local privilege escalation rather than just configuration tampering.
Writable HKCU key that, while lower severity on its own, still enables tampering with security-relevant per-user settings (proxy config, update source).
mitigation: Set registry key DACLs so only Administrators/SYSTEM have write access; grant the application's own service account the minimum write access it genuinely needs rather than opening the key to all users.
Move genuinely per-user, non-security-relevant settings to HKCU rather than a shared HKLM location writable by everyone.
Audit installer-created ACLs as part of the release process rather than relying on Windows default inheritance to be sufficiently restrictive.
Where a privileged service reads configuration from a location, validate and sanity-check that configuration defensively rather than trusting it implicitly.

items.title: Default/Weak Database Credentials (Embedded DB)
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. Knowledge of the embedded database engine in use (SQLite, Firebird, embedded MySQL/PostgreSQL, or a proprietary engine) and its default client tooling for direct connection attempts.
items.whatItIs: The app comes bundled with its own local database, and that database still has the vendor's default admin username and password — the ones printed right in the installation guide — because the setup process never asks you to change them.
items.rootCause: Setting up the database is treated as just a technical installation step, not something with security implications. So the vendor's default password — which is often public knowledge, since it's in their own documentation — ships unchanged into every install unless an administrator happens to remember to change it manually.
items.impact: Any local user can log straight into the bundled database using the documented default credential. Where the database is also misconfigured to listen beyond the local machine, anyone on the network can do the same. Either way they bypass the application's access control and business logic entirely, reading, modifying or extracting the underlying data directly.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the embedded database engine and version from installed files/service names, and consult the vendor's public installation documentation for any default account it creates.
Check whether the database service binds to localhost only or is reachable over the network (netstat/ss for listening ports bound to 0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1).
Attempt to connect using the vendor's documented default credential with the appropriate client tool for that database engine.
If direct default-credential login fails, check the application's own configuration/connection-string files for a stored, potentially still-default, credential in cleartext or weakly encoded form.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes direct database connection attempts against the test installation's embedded database.
Attempt authentication using the documented vendor default username/password against the local database instance.

If successful, enumerate accessible schemas/tables to confirm the scope of data reachable (customer records, credentials, financial data) as proof of impact, without exfiltrating real production data if this is tested against a live instance.
If the database is also network-reachable, repeat the connection attempt from a separate network-adjacent test host to demonstrate the broader exposure beyond local-only risk.
Document the exact default credential used, the database engine/version, and the binding scope (local-only vs. network-reachable) for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Check for network-reachable database listener
Attempt default-credential login (example: embedded MySQL)
Attempt default-credential login (example: SQLite with app-level auth wrapper)
examplePayloads.command: sqlite3 app_data.db ".tables"  # confirm whether the file itself is unencrypted and directly readable

variants: Embedded database with no authentication at all (rather than a weak default), where any local process can connect without any credential.

Default credential still valid on the database even though the application's own UI-layer login has been properly configured with unique per-customer credentials — the database layer bypass renders the UI-layer control moot.
mitigation: Force a mandatory, unique credential to be set for the embedded database during first-run setup, refusing to start the application until the default has been changed.
Bind the embedded database to localhost only unless network access is an explicit, documented requirement, and firewall the port regardless as defense in depth.

Encrypt the database file at rest (e.g. SQLCipher for SQLite-based clients) so direct file access without the application's own credential/key doesn't trivially expose data even if the network/local-access vector is closed.
Include a default-credential check in the vendor's own release/deployment checklist and in this VAPT's recurring test cycle.

items.title: Insecure Auto-Login Credential Caching
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, with the auto-login/remember-me feature enabled during setup. Tools to inspect the credential storage location: registry viewer, file/config inspector, or a memory-dump/decompilation tool if the credential is embedded in application state rather than persisted to disk.
items.whatItIs: The app has a 'remember me' or auto-login feature that saves your password (or an equivalent secret) locally so you don't have to log in every time. But that saved value is stored in plain text, or 'scrambled' in a way that's trivial to reverse (like Base64 or a simple XOR), or protected by an encryption key that's baked right into the app itself or easily derivable from basic details of the machine it's running on.
items.rootCause: This feature was built purely to skip the login screen for convenience, without considering that any other user, process, or piece of malware on the same computer can read that same saved file or registry entry. The local machine was wrongly assumed to be a fully trusted, private space.
items.impact: Any other process or account with read access to the machine can recover the cached credential and impersonate the legitimate user against the backend. They never need to compromise the network or the backend itself. That turns a single-machine compromise, or merely shared access to a multi-user machine, into full account takeover.
stepsToIdentify: Enable the auto-login/remember-me feature and locate where the resulting credential material is written (registry, a config/INI file, an app-data folder) using Process Monitor to capture the write operation as it happens.
Inspect the stored value directly: attempt Base64 decoding, check for a fixed/short XOR key, or attempt to load it with a common weak-encryption routine before assuming it's properly protected.

If the value appears encrypted, decompile the application to locate the decryption routine and determine whether the key is hardcoded, derived from a static machine identifier (predictable), or genuinely tied to a user/OS-level secret store (DPAPI, Keychain, or an OS-level credential manager) that provides real protection.
Test access to the cached value from a second, separate user account on the same machine to confirm whether OS-level file/registry permissions provide any compensating protection.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes local credential-caching analysis against the test installation.
Locate and extract the cached credential material from its storage location.
Attempt to decode/decrypt the value using the routine identified via decompilation (or straightforward Base64/XOR if no real protection is present).

Use the recovered credential to authenticate directly against the backend (or demonstrate that simply copying the cached file/registry value to a second machine and launching the application there logs in automatically) as proof of impact.
Document exactly what protection (if any) was applied and how trivially it was reversed, since this materially affects the severity/remediation-priority narrative.

examplePayloads.label: Capture the credential-cache write during first login
Attempt straightforward decode of the cached value
Decompile to locate the decrypt routine and key source
examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app.exe  # search for Decrypt/UnprotectCredential/XOR-style helper functions

examplePayloads.label: Confirm portability of the cached credential to a second machine/user

variants: Session-token caching (rather than the raw password) that is still long-lived and unbound to the original machine, giving equivalent impact to password caching.
Reliance on a genuine OS-level secret store (DPAPI/Keychain) that is nonetheless still readable by any process running as the same OS user account, which narrows but doesn't eliminate the exposure.
mitigation: Use the platform's proper credential-storage API (Windows DPAPI/Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, a Linux Secret Service implementation) rather than a custom or reversible encoding scheme, and scope access to the specific application.
Prefer short-lived, revocable session tokens over cached passwords, with server-side revocation available if a machine is reported lost/compromised.
Bind any cached credential material to machine-specific, non-exportable key material (e.g. a TPM-backed key) so copying the cache file to another machine doesn't grant access there.
Make the auto-login/remember-me feature opt-in with a clear warning about the tradeoff, rather than a default-on convenience setting.

items.title: Client-Side Authorization/Trust Boundary Violation
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A debugger or hooking framework (x64dbg, Frida, or a .NET-specific tool like dnSpy's built-in debugger) capable of modifying in-memory variables or intercepting function calls at runtime, and a network proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) if the client also communicates with a backend to re-verify tampered decisions server-side.
items.whatItIs: The app decides, entirely on its own — whether a feature is unlocked, whether a transaction is allowed, whether you're an admin — without the server double-checking that decision independently. It trusts what the client-side code says, instead of treating the client as just a display layer and making the real decision on the server.
items.rootCause: The app puts a decision that needs to be trustworthy inside code the end user fully controls, can inspect, and can modify while it's running — instead of inside server-side code the user has no access to. A client can ask the server to do something, but it should never be the thing that decides whether that request is actually allowed.
items.impact: A user, or malware acting on their behalf, can bypass licence tiers, unlock premium features, raise their own effective privilege inside the application, or approve transactions the server would have refused. All of it is achieved by patching local state or the binary. No valid credential for the elevated action is ever required.
stepsToIdentify: Map every authorization-relevant decision point in the application (feature gating, role checks, transaction approval) and determine, for each, whether the client independently decides or whether it merely reflects a decision the server also separately enforces.

Attach a debugger to a running instance and set breakpoints on functions that appear to check a boolean/enum representing entitlement or role (e.g. IsAdmin, IsLicensed, MaxTransactionLimit) to see whether flipping the value in memory changes application behavior without any server round-trip.

Proxy the application's network traffic while performing the same tampered action to confirm whether the server independently validates and rejects the action, or silently accepts whatever the client asserts.
Check configuration/license files for locally-stored entitlement flags that the client reads and trusts without any signature or server-side confirmation.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes runtime memory patching and/or binary modification of the test installation.

Identify the in-memory variable or function controlling the target authorization decision using a debugger, and modify it at runtime (or patch the corresponding conditional jump in the binary) to force the elevated/unlocked state.
Attempt the previously-restricted action (unlock a premium feature, submit a transaction above the client-enforced limit, access an admin-only menu) and observe whether it succeeds locally.

Simultaneously proxy the network traffic to confirm whether the backend independently rejects the action despite the client believing it succeeded, which determines whether this is a cosmetic client bug or an exploitable authorization bypass with real business impact.
Document the specific decision point, the patching technique used, and — critically — whether server-side validation caught or missed the tampered request.

examplePayloads.label: Attach a debugger and search for entitlement-check functions
examplePayloads.command: x64dbg target_app.exe  # set breakpoint on IsLicensed/IsAdmin-style function, modify return value

examplePayloads.label: Frida-based runtime hook to force a function's return value
examplePayloads.command: frida -n target_app -l force_true.js  # force_true.js: Interceptor.replace(IsLicensedAddr, ...) returning 1

examplePayloads.label: Proxy traffic during the tampered action to check server-side re-validation

variants: License/entitlement bypass by patching a locally-stored license file's signature check rather than live memory.
Transaction-limit bypass in a financial/trading thick client where a client-enforced maximum is trivially raised via memory patching, with the server accepting whatever the client submits.
mitigation: Move every security- and business-relevant authorization decision to the server; treat the client exclusively as a presentation layer that requests actions, never one that approves them.
Independently re-validate entitlements, roles, and transaction limits server-side on every request, regardless of what the client's local state claims.
Where offline/local functionality is genuinely required, use cryptographically signed entitlement tokens that the client cannot forge, verified against a key the client doesn't possess.
Add anti-tampering/integrity-check mechanisms as a defense-in-depth layer, understanding that they raise the bar but cannot substitute for proper server-side enforcement.

items.title: Improper Privilege Escalation (Updater/Service)
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application (including its auto-updater or companion service) on a test machine you control, with standard non-administrative user access. Sysinternals Process Monitor and accesschk, plus a disassembler if the updater's validation logic needs inspection.
items.whatItIs: The app's auto-updater or a background service runs with full admin/SYSTEM privileges so it can install updates. But the way a regular, non-admin user triggers or feeds it input isn't locked down enough — so a low-privileged user can manipulate what that powerful updater actually ends up doing.
items.rootCause: The split between the regular app (low privilege) and the elevated updater (high privilege) was designed for convenience — users shouldn't need an admin password just to get an update. But the connection between the two — a shared file, folder, or scheduled task the elevated part reads from — is still writable by the regular, low-privilege user, which erases the whole point of separating them.
items.impact: A standard non-administrative user can make the privileged updater or service execute code they control, with SYSTEM or root privileges. They might deliver it as a malicious update package, a tampered configuration file, or a spoofed message to the service. The result is complete local privilege escalation from an ordinary starting point.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the privileged component (service name, scheduled task, or elevated helper process) associated with the application's update mechanism using Process Explorer/Task Manager to confirm its running privilege level.

Trace the IPC channel or shared resource (named pipe, shared folder, scheduled task definition, registry key) through which the standard-privilege UI communicates with or feeds the privileged component, using Process Monitor.
Check the permissions on that shared resource for standard-user write access using accesschk.
Review whether the privileged component validates the authenticity/integrity of whatever it receives from the standard-privilege side (a signed update package check) or trusts it implicitly.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes local privilege-escalation testing against the test installation's update mechanism.
As a standard user, write or substitute a malicious payload into the identified shared resource (a fake update package, a tampered IPC message, a modified scheduled-task argument).
Trigger the privileged component to consume the tampered input (initiate a manual update check, wait for the scheduled task, or restart the service).

Confirm code execution occurs in the elevated component's context by observing a benign proof-of-concept action (spawning a process, writing a file to a location a standard user couldn't otherwise write to) running with SYSTEM/root privileges.
Document the exact IPC/shared-resource path, its permissions, and the missing validation step that allowed the tampered input to be trusted.

examplePayloads.label: Trace IPC/shared-resource usage by the privileged updater
Check permissions on the discovered shared resource
Substitute a benign proof-of-concept payload as a standard user
Trigger the privileged component to consume the payload

variants: Update package signature verification present but weak/bypassable (e.g. checking only a filename pattern rather than a cryptographic signature).
Scheduled-task-based updater where the task's binary path or arguments are writable by standard users rather than the update payload itself.
mitigation: Apply least-privilege ACLs to every file, folder, registry key, and IPC channel the privileged updater/service reads from or is triggered by, restricting write access to administrators only.
Cryptographically sign update packages and verify the signature against a pinned, non-user-writable public key before the privileged component acts on them.
Validate and sanitize all input the privileged component receives from any lower-privileged source, treating it as untrusted regardless of the IPC mechanism used.

Where feasible, minimize what the elevated component actually does — perform as much processing as possible in a properly-privileged, sandboxed step rather than granting broad SYSTEM/root scope to the entire updater.

links: CWE-732 (Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource)
CWE-494 (Download of Code Without Integrity Check)

items.title: Local Privilege Escalation via Insecure Service Permissions
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, standard (non-administrative) user access, and Sysinternals accesschk/PowerUp or WinPEAS for enumeration. A disassembler/decompiler (dnSpy, Ghidra) if the service binary itself (rather than just its file-system permissions) needs inspection.
items.whatItIs: A Windows service the app installs runs as SYSTEM (the highest privilege level), but the file and registry permissions protecting its program file or configuration are too loose — letting a regular, non-admin user replace the service's executable file or change what it actually launches.
items.rootCause: The installer sets weak permissions on the folder holding the service's file, or its registry configuration — often because the folder just inherited permissive settings from its parent, or the installer deliberately allowed regular users to modify it to make future updates easier. Nobody accounted for the fact that write access to a file SYSTEM will run is the same as SYSTEM-level access itself.
items.impact: A standard non-administrative user can replace the service's program file, or repoint its registry entry to something else. They then trigger a restart, or simply wait for the next boot. Their code runs with SYSTEM privileges. That is a complete local privilege escalation from an unprivileged start.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all services installed by the application and their run-as account using `sc qc <servicename>` or Services.msc, flagging any running as SYSTEM or a similarly privileged account.
Run accesschk against each service's binary path, containing folder, and registry ImagePath value to check for standard-user write access.
Run PowerUp or WinPEAS as a standard user for an automated sweep that cross-references all of the above and flags exploitable services directly.
Where the binary path itself is correctly locked down, separately check whether the service loads any DLL from a writable, non-standard search-path location (overlaps with the DLL-hijacking finding).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes local privilege-escalation testing against the target service.
As a standard user, replace the service's binary (or modify its ImagePath registry value to point at a payload you control) using the write access identified during discovery.
Restart the service (`sc stop`/`sc start`, or trigger a reboot if the service is boot-start) to execute the payload with the service's elevated privileges.

Confirm privilege escalation succeeded via a benign proof-of-concept (e.g. the payload writes a file to a SYSTEM-only-writable location, or spawns a process visibly running as SYSTEM in Task Manager).
Restore the original service binary/configuration after the proof-of-concept and document the exact vulnerable path and permission entry.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate service run-as account and binary path
Automated privilege-escalation sweep
Check specific ACL on the service binary/folder
Modify a writable ImagePath to point at a test payload

variants: Weak registry permission on the service's ImagePath value specifically, distinct from a weak file-system permission on the binary itself.
Unquoted service path vulnerability, where a space in an unquoted binary path lets a standard user plant an executable earlier in the resolved path sequence.
mitigation: Apply least-privilege file-system and registry ACLs to all service-related paths during installation, restricting write access to Administrators/SYSTEM only.
Quote all service binary paths containing spaces to eliminate the unquoted-path variant of this issue.
Audit installer-created service permissions as a standing release-gate check, since this class of bug commonly regresses across product versions/updates.

Apply the principle of least privilege to the service's run-as account itself where SYSTEM is not genuinely required — a dedicated, lower-privileged service account limits the blast radius even if a permission weakness is later found.

items.title: Insecure Deserialization (Thick Client)
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A decompiler appropriate to the runtime (dnSpy/ILSpy for .NET's BinaryFormatter, ysoserial.net for .NET gadget chains, ysoserial for Java, or a Python pickle-specific analysis approach). A proxy/interception point on whatever channel carries the serialized object (IPC, a local file, or network traffic to a companion service).
items.whatItIs: The app loads saved data (from a file, a message between processes, or network traffic) using a format (like .NET's BinaryFormatter, Java's native serialization, or Python's pickle) that can reconstruct any kind of object the data describes — not just simple, safe data. If an attacker can control or tamper with that saved data, they can craft a malicious object that runs their own code the moment it gets loaded.
items.rootCause: These formats work by directly building whatever object type the data says to build, running its setup code along the way — with no restriction on which types are allowed. If the app has other, unrelated classes loaded that can be chained together in unexpected ways, an attacker can use that chain to run arbitrary code. Any untrusted data reaching this kind of loading function is a direct path to code execution.
items.impact: An attacker who can supply or tamper with the serialised data achieves arbitrary code execution inside the process that loads it, which is usually the full application privilege level. The data might arrive as a tampered save file, a message from another local process, a modified response from a companion service, or a crafted file the application imports.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and search for use of type-permissive native serializers (BinaryFormatter, NetDataContractSerializer, Java ObjectInputStream, Python pickle.loads) rather than a safe, schema-constrained format (JSON, protobuf).
Trace each call site back to its data source: a local save/config file, an IPC channel, or network traffic, and assess how directly an attacker can control or tamper with that source.
Check whether any type-allowlisting (a SerializationBinder in .NET, an ObjectInputFilter in Java) is in place restricting deserialization to expected types.
Where a serialized payload is found in a local file or captured IPC/network traffic, save a sample for use with a public gadget-chain generation tool during the exploitation phase.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes deserialization-based code-execution testing against the test installation.
Identify the exact serializer and runtime version in use via decompilation, since gadget-chain availability depends on which assemblies are loaded.
Generate a malicious serialized payload using a public gadget-chain tool (ysoserial.net for .NET, ysoserial for Java) targeting a gadget chain compatible with the application's loaded assemblies.
Deliver the malicious payload via the identified data path (replace a local save file, inject via the IPC channel, or modify a network response from a companion service) and trigger deserialization.
Confirm code execution via a benign proof-of-concept command (e.g. spawning calc.exe or writing a test file) and document the exact gadget chain and delivery vector used.

examplePayloads.label: Search decompiled code for permissive deserialization calls
examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app.exe  # search assembly for BinaryFormatter.Deserialize / NetDataContractSerializer

examplePayloads.label: Generate a .NET gadget-chain payload
Generate a Java gadget-chain payload
Deliver the payload by replacing a local save/state file

variants: Deserialization triggered via a local file (save state, plugin config) versus via network/IPC traffic from a companion process — the former requires local file-write access, the latter can be remote if the companion channel is network-reachable.
Partial mitigation present (a SerializationBinder allowlist) that is itself bypassable due to an overly broad type-name pattern match.
mitigation: Replace type-permissive native serializers with a safe, schema-constrained format (JSON with a strict schema, protobuf) wherever the application controls both ends of the serialization.

Where native serialization cannot be avoided, implement a strict type-allowlist (SerializationBinder/ObjectInputFilter) permitting only the specific, minimal set of types the application actually needs to deserialize.
Never deserialize data from an untrusted or externally-writable source without independent integrity verification (a signature over the serialized bytes, checked before deserialization begins).
Keep the application's dependency set minimal and current, since gadget-chain availability depends heavily on which library versions are loaded.

items.title: Runtime Manipulation (Hooking/Injection)
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A runtime instrumentation/hooking framework (Frida, x64dbg with scripting, or Detours for native DLL injection) and a disassembler to identify target functions for hooking.
items.whatItIs: The app makes important security decisions — checking a license, detecting tampering, approving a transaction, generating an encryption key — inside functions that can be intercepted and changed while the program is running, using standard, well-known tools (injecting code into the process, hooking specific functions, using tools like Frida to modify behavior live). Nothing in the app detects or resists this kind of live tampering.
items.rootCause: The app assumes its own running code and memory can be trusted and won't be interfered with. But on a regular computer, an app has no special protection from a user (or malware) with normal permissions — without active defenses built in, every function call and stored value can be inspected and changed by anyone running the program.
items.impact: An attacker can hook or patch any function whose behaviour they want to change. They can force a licence check to always return valid, intercept an encryption routine to capture keys and plaintext before encryption happens, or alter a business decision outright. Critically, they do not need to understand the application's internal logic, because the hook operates at the function boundary rather than requiring a deep binary patch.
stepsToIdentify: Attempt to attach a standard debugger (x64dbg, WinDbg) or Frida to a running instance of the application and observe whether any anti-debugging/anti-attach countermeasure triggers (process termination, integrity-check failure, or silent behavioral change).
Identify security-relevant functions via decompilation (license checks, crypto routines, business-logic gates) and attempt to set a hook/breakpoint on each to confirm they're interceptable.
Check whether the binary employs any packing, obfuscation, or checksum/integrity self-verification that would need to be defeated before hooking is straightforward.
Assess whether the application performs any environment checks (detecting known hooking-framework artifacts, virtualization, or a debugger process) as a baseline anti-tampering posture.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes runtime hooking/injection testing against the test installation.
Attach the chosen hooking framework to the running application and confirm it doesn't detect or resist the attach.
Hook the identified security-relevant function (e.g. the license-validation routine) and force its return value to the desired outcome.
Demonstrate the resulting bypass by exercising the previously-restricted functionality (an unlocked premium feature, a bypassed anti-cheat check, an intercepted encryption key) as proof of concept.
Document which specific function(s) were hookable, the absence (or presence and bypass) of any anti-tampering countermeasure, and the resulting business impact.

examplePayloads.label: Attach Frida and list exported/interesting functions
Hook a license-check function to force a true return value
examplePayloads.command: frida -n target_app -l hook_license_check.js  # Interceptor.attach(LicenseCheckAddr, { onLeave: retval => retval.replace(1) })

examplePayloads.label: Attach a native debugger and set a breakpoint on the target routine
examplePayloads.command: x64dbg target_app.exe  # bp on decompiled address of IsLicenseValid

variants: DLL injection into the target process to run arbitrary code within its address space, versus lighter-weight API hooking that only intercepts specific calls.
Anti-tampering present but bypassable (e.g. a debugger-detection check that only looks for one specific debugger's window class name).
mitigation: Move genuinely security-critical decisions (license validation, transaction approval) server-side wherever feasible, so client-side hooking has nothing sensitive to intercept (overlaps with the client-side-trust-boundary finding).

Where local, offline enforcement is unavoidable, adopt runtime application self-protection (RASP), code obfuscation, and integrity self-checks to raise the cost of hooking, understanding this raises the bar rather than providing an absolute guarantee.
Implement anti-debugging and anti-injection countermeasures (detecting known hooking-framework artifacts, verifying own code-segment checksums at runtime) as defense in depth.
Accept that determined, well-resourced attackers can defeat client-side anti-tampering given enough time; prioritize server-side enforcement for anything with real financial or security consequence.

items.title: Business Logic Bypass via Client Tampering
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) capable of capturing and replaying/modifying the client-server traffic that carries the business-logic-relevant request. Optionally, a debugger for cases where the tamperable value lives only in client memory rather than in a network request.
items.whatItIs: A business rule — like a maximum discount, an order limit, or a required approval step — is enforced mainly (or only) on the client side. Someone who intercepts and edits the outgoing request, or directly modifies the app's own in-memory data, can submit something that breaks the rule, and the server accepts it without checking again itself.
items.rootCause: The rule was built as a UI convenience — greying out a button, capping what you can type into a field — under the assumption that people would only ever use the official app interface. There's no independent, matching check on the server, which is the only place that actually controls the real data change.
items.impact: A user can bypass the intended business rule entirely — applying a discount beyond the authorised maximum, ordering beyond stock or credit limits, or skipping a required approval step. What that costs depends on the rule broken, ranging from direct financial loss to a broken workflow or a downstream compliance problem.
stepsToIdentify: Map the application's business rules (discount caps, quantity limits, approval gates, workflow ordering) and, for each, determine whether the client merely reflects a UI convenience or is the sole enforcement point.
Proxy the client's traffic while performing a normal, rule-compliant action to understand the exact request format the server expects.
Attempt to submit a rule-violating value directly via the proxy (bypassing the client UI's own input restrictions) and observe whether the server accepts or rejects it.

For rules enforced purely in client memory (not reflected in any network request field), use a debugger to locate and modify the relevant in-memory value, then observe whether the resulting action still succeeds server-side.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes business-logic tampering tests against the test installation and a non-production backend/test account.
Capture a legitimate, rule-compliant request via the proxy to establish the baseline request structure and expected field values.

Modify the captured request to violate the identified business rule (e.g. increase a discount field beyond the client-enforced cap, submit a quantity beyond the displayed maximum) and replay it to the server.

If the rule is enforced only via a disabled/grayed-out UI element rather than a request field limit, use a debugger to force the underlying value past its intended bound before the request is constructed, then proxy and confirm server acceptance.
Document exactly which rule was bypassed, the resulting server-side effect, and whether any server-side validation existed at all or was simply insufficient.

examplePayloads.label: Capture and replay a modified request bypassing a client-enforced limit
examplePayloads.command: # In Burp Repeater: change discountPercent=15 (client max) to discountPercent=75, resend

examplePayloads.label: Locate and patch an in-memory business-rule variable
examplePayloads.command: x64dbg target_app.exe  # find MaxOrderQuantity variable, patch to a higher value before request construction

examplePayloads.label: Automated fuzzing of a business-logic-relevant field for boundary handling

variants: Workflow-ordering bypass, where a multi-step approval process can have its steps submitted out of order or skipped entirely if the server doesn't track and enforce workflow state itself.
Client-enforced numeric cap bypassed via direct request field modification, distinct from an in-memory-only variable that never appears in any request field at all.
mitigation: Re-implement every business-relevant rule as an independent, authoritative server-side check; treat all client-side versions of the same rule as UX convenience only, never as enforcement.
Validate the full context of a request server-side (prior workflow state, current entitlements, computed limits) rather than trusting any client-supplied value that represents a rule outcome.
Log and alert on server-side rule violations that shouldn't be reachable via the official client UI, since their occurrence is a strong indicator of exactly this kind of tampering in production.
Include boundary and out-of-order-workflow test cases in the standard QA/regression suite so business-logic bypass regressions are caught before release, not just during periodic VAPT engagements.

links: OWASP WSTG-BUSL-01 (Test Business Logic Data Validation)

items.title: Missing Certificate Pinning
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) with its CA certificate available for installation, and a means to redirect the application's traffic through the proxy (system proxy settings or a transparent network configuration).
items.whatItIs: The app talks to its server over HTTPS, but doesn't check that the server's certificate is specifically the one it expects — it just trusts anything the operating system's built-in list of trusted certificate authorities accepts. That means a certificate from any authority the OS trusts (including one a tester or attacker controls, or one installed by tricking the user) will be accepted, letting someone sit in the middle of that 'secure' connection.
items.rootCause: Pinning the expected certificate (locking the app to trust only the real server's specific certificate) wasn't implemented, because it adds ongoing maintenance work — updating the pin whenever the certificate is renewed, handling failures gracefully — and that complexity was judged not worth it. So the app's trust decision falls back entirely to the OS's general trust list instead of something narrower and app-specific.
items.impact: An attacker on the network path can silently read and modify all traffic between the client and its backend, including credentials, session tokens and business data. They might be running a malicious proxy, sitting on a compromised Wi-Fi network, or relying on a rogue certificate installed on the victim's machine. The client shows no warning at any point.
stepsToIdentify: Install the testing proxy's CA certificate into the OS trust store on the test machine and configure the application's network traffic to route through the proxy.
Launch the application and attempt to use any network-dependent feature (login, data sync, an API call) while observing the proxy for successfully decrypted traffic.
If traffic is visible in the proxy without any application-level warning or connection failure, certificate pinning is absent or ineffective.

Where a pinning implementation does exist, test whether it can be bypassed via known techniques (hooking the pin-validation function with Frida, patching the binary to skip the check) to assess implementation robustness rather than just presence.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes MITM proxy testing against the test installation's network traffic.
Install the proxy's CA certificate into the test machine's trust store and route the application's traffic through the intercepting proxy.
Perform a normal, sensitive action within the application (login, a data-sensitive API call) and confirm the proxy captures the decrypted request/response content.
Document the specific sensitive data observed in the intercepted traffic (credentials, tokens, business data) as the impact evidence.
If pinning is present but suspected to be weak, attempt a Frida-based bypass of the pin-validation function and repeat the interception to demonstrate the bypass.

examplePayloads.label: Route application traffic through an intercepting proxy
examplePayloads.command: # configure system/app proxy settings to 127.0.0.1:8080 and install Burp's CA cert into the OS trust store

examplePayloads.label: Confirm interception of a login/API call
examplePayloads.command: # observe decrypted request/response in Burp's HTTP history for the target application's traffic

examplePayloads.label: Frida-based bypass of an existing (weak) pinning implementation
examplePayloads.command: frida -n target_app -l universal-android-ssl-pinning-bypass.js  # or an equivalent desktop-specific unpinning script

variants: Pinning implemented but only checking the certificate's Common Name/SAN rather than the full certificate or public key, making it bypassable with a certificate for any domain issued by a trusted CA.
Pinning present in the primary connection but absent on a secondary channel (a telemetry/crash-reporting endpoint, an update-check call) that still carries sensitive data.
mitigation: Implement certificate or public-key pinning for all backend connections, validating against a pinned value embedded in the client rather than relying solely on OS trust-store validation.
Pin the public key (SPKI hash) rather than the full certificate where possible, so certificate renewal doesn't require a client update as long as the key is reused.
Implement a pin-rotation/backup-pin strategy to avoid bricking clients on legitimate certificate changes, and monitor for pin-validation failures in production as a potential MITM indicator.
Apply pinning consistently across every network endpoint the client communicates with, not just the primary authentication/API channel.

links: CWE-297 (Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch)
OWASP WSTG-CRYP-03 (Test for Sensitive Information Sent via Unencrypted Channels)

items.title: Weak Local Cryptography / Key Management
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A decompiler/disassembler (dnSpy/ILSpy, Ghidra, IDA) to locate cryptographic routines and key material, and a hex editor or memory-inspection tool to examine key storage locations directly.
items.whatItIs: The app encrypts sensitive local data (saved credentials, cached business data, license info), but manages the encryption key poorly — hardcoding it directly in the program, deriving it from something predictable (like the computer's name), or storing it right next to the data it's supposed to protect. However strong the encryption algorithm is, none of that matters if the key is this easy to recover.
items.rootCause: Good key management — generating it securely, storing it separately from the data, ideally using the OS's built-in secure storage — was treated as an afterthought compared to just 'using encryption' as a checkbox. The algorithm might be fine, but encryption is only as strong as how well its key is protected, and here it isn't.
items.impact: An attacker can decrypt all the protected local data regardless of how strong the encryption algorithm is on paper. There are three routes, depending on the flaw: decompile the binary to lift a hardcoded key, repeat the same derivation the application performs, or simply read the key from the same place the encrypted data sits. The algorithm is never the weak point here — the key handling is.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and search for cryptographic API calls (AES/DES/RSA initialization) and trace backward to identify where the key parameter originates.

Check whether the key is a literal string/byte array embedded in the binary, computed from a static or easily-obtainable value (machine name, a fixed salt), or retrieved from a genuine OS-level secret store.
If the key is derived, attempt to replicate the derivation independently using only publicly-obtainable inputs to confirm real-world recoverability.
Check whether the key (or its derivation inputs) is stored in the same file/registry location as the encrypted data itself, which would allow full compromise from a single artifact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cryptographic-implementation analysis of the test installation.
Decompile the application to locate the exact key material or derivation routine used for local data encryption.
Extract or independently recompute the key using the identified method.
Use the recovered key to decrypt a sample of the application's locally-stored protected data (a cached credential, business data file) as proof of concept.
Document the exact key-management weakness (hardcoded, weakly derived, co-located with ciphertext) since remediation differs materially between these variants.

examplePayloads.label: Search decompiled code for hardcoded key material
examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app.exe  # search for byte[] literals near AES/Rijndael/DES initialization calls

examplePayloads.label: Extract and use a recovered key to decrypt local data
examplePayloads.command: python3 -c "from Crypto.Cipher import AES; ..."  # decrypt a captured local data file using the extracted key/IV

examplePayloads.label: Check whether key material is co-located with the ciphertext file
examplePayloads.command: dir /a "%APPDATA%\<App>\"  # confirm whether a key file sits alongside the encrypted data file

variants: Hardcoded key shared identically across every installation of the application, meaning a single successful extraction compromises every customer's data, not just the tested instance.
Weak key derivation from a machine-specific but still low-entropy or guessable value (e.g. a hash of just the computer name).
mitigation: Never hardcode encryption keys in the binary; use a properly random, per-installation key generated at first run.

Store the key using the platform's genuine hardware- or OS-backed secret store (Windows DPAPI/TPM, macOS Keychain/Secure Enclave), not in a location co-located with or derivable from the protected data.
If key derivation from user input (a master password) is used, apply a proper KDF (PBKDF2/Argon2/scrypt) with an adequate work factor rather than a single fast hash.
Conduct a key-management-specific review as part of every cryptography-related code change, since this class of weakness commonly hides behind an otherwise correctly-chosen algorithm.

items.title: Weak Obfuscation of License Key Validation Algorithm
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A decompiler/disassembler suited to the runtime (dnSpy/ILSpy for .NET, Ghidra/IDA for native code) and, where present, a de-obfuscation tool (de4dot for common .NET obfuscators) to reverse whatever obfuscation layer protects the license-check routine.
items.whatItIs: The app's license-checking logic relies purely on making the code hard to read (scrambled names, tangled logic, encrypted strings) instead of a real, server-verified, cryptographically signed license the client can't fake. Once that obfuscation is undone — a mostly automated, well-tooled process for common obfuscators — the license check is fully readable and editable.
items.rootCause: Obfuscation makes code harder to read, but it doesn't make it impossible, and it provides no actual cryptographic guarantee against forgery. It was chosen as the only protection under the mistaken belief that 'harder to read' is the same as 'can't be bypassed' — but a motivated attacker, or even an existing public tool for that specific obfuscator, can undo it with fairly bounded effort.
items.impact: Once the obfuscation is unwound, the licence check can be patched in the binary so it always passes. Alternatively the validation algorithm itself becomes clear, and an attacker can generate keys that look genuine. Either way the product loses control of its licensing and entitlement revenue entirely.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the obfuscation tool/technique in use (via characteristic renamed-symbol patterns, known obfuscator signatures, or metadata artifacts) and check for publicly available de-obfuscation tooling targeting it.
Attempt de-obfuscation using the identified tool and assess how much of the original logic (particularly the license-validation routine) becomes readable.
Locate the license-validation function post-de-obfuscation and determine whether it validates against any server-side signal at all, or is a purely local/offline algorithmic check.
Assess whether the validation algorithm, once readable, is straightforward enough to reverse-engineer into a standalone key-generation routine.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes reverse-engineering and patching of the license-validation logic in the test installation.
De-obfuscate the binary using the identified tool/technique.
Locate and analyze the license-validation function to understand its exact validation algorithm.

Demonstrate impact via either (a) binary-patching the validation check to force a "valid" result regardless of the actual license state, or (b) reconstructing the validation algorithm well enough to generate a syntactically valid license key for a license the tester does not hold.
Document the specific obfuscation technique defeated, the tooling used, and the resulting bypass method for the report.

examplePayloads.label: De-obfuscate a common .NET obfuscator's output
Locate the license-check routine post-de-obfuscation
examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app_deobfuscated.exe  # search for 'License', 'Validate', 'Entitlement' near string-comparison logic

examplePayloads.label: Binary-patch the validation check to force success
examplePayloads.command: # in dnSpy: edit the IL of the validation method to always return true, save the modified assembly

variants: Obfuscated but purely local/offline license-key algorithm that, once reversed, allows generation of unlimited valid-looking keys without any server contact at all.
Obfuscation combined with a genuine server-side check for some features but not others, so only partial functionality is protected once the local check is bypassed.
mitigation: Treat obfuscation as a raise-the-cost measure only, never as the sole protection for anything with real business/financial value; pair it with genuine server-side license verification wherever feasible.
Implement license validation as a cryptographically signed token issued and periodically re-validated by a server the client cannot impersonate, rather than a purely local algorithmic check.

Where offline/local validation is a genuine business requirement (air-gapped environments), use asymmetric cryptography (the client only holds a public key, unable to generate valid signatures itself) rather than a symmetric or purely algorithmic scheme.
Accept that a sufficiently motivated attacker will eventually defeat any purely client-side protection, and design the licensing model's risk tolerance accordingly.

items.title: Client-Side Rate Limiting Bypass via Direct API Call (Thick Client)
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) capable of replaying captured requests directly to the backend API, bypassing the client UI entirely.
items.whatItIs: The app's interface limits how often you can try something sensitive — like logging in or requesting a password reset — by disabling a button or adding a delay. But the actual server the app talks to has no matching limit of its own. So someone who skips the app entirely and calls the server directly can attempt the action as fast as their network connection allows.
items.rootCause: Rate limiting was built purely as a nice user experience in the app (stop people from spamming the button) instead of as a real security control on the server — the one place an attacker actually can't route around. The server just assumed every request would come from the properly-throttled app.
items.impact: An attacker can brute-force credentials, one-time codes, or any other rate-sensitive value at full speed by calling the backend API directly. The client-side throttle never applies, because the client is no longer involved. What appears to be a rate-limited login or verification flow has, in practice, no limit at all.
stepsToIdentify: Proxy the client's traffic while performing the rate-limited action normally and identify the exact API endpoint/request the client calls.

Replay the captured request directly and repeatedly via the proxy (bypassing the client UI entirely) and observe whether the server processes each attempt without any throttling, lockout, or CAPTCHA challenge appearing.
Measure how many attempts can be sent before any server-side control (if any) engages, to quantify the real-world brute-force feasibility.
Check whether the endpoint returns any distinguishing response (timing difference, error message variance) that could aid a targeted brute-force attack even if raw rate isn't unlimited.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes direct API brute-force testing against a non-production backend/test account.
Capture the exact request structure for the rate-limited action via the proxy.
Use an automated tool (Burp Intruder, a custom script) to replay the request at high volume directly against the backend, bypassing the client application entirely.

Confirm whether the server processes an unrestricted (or much higher than intended) number of attempts, and, if targeting an authentication flow, whether a valid credential/OTP can be identified via this direct brute-force within a reasonable time budget.
Document the exact absence (or insufficiency) of server-side rate limiting as the core finding, distinct from the cosmetic client-side throttle.

examplePayloads.label: Capture the rate-limited request via proxy
examplePayloads.command: # perform one login/OTP attempt through the client with Burp intercepting, save the request

examplePayloads.label: Replay the captured request at high volume, bypassing the client throttle
examplePayloads.command: # Burp Intruder: load captured request, sniper attack on the credential/OTP field, no client-side delay applied

examplePayloads.label: Scripted direct API brute-force

variants: OTP/verification-code brute-force where the code space is small enough (a 4-6 digit numeric code) that unrestricted attempts make full brute-force practical within minutes.
Password-reset-token brute-force following the same client-throttle-only pattern.
mitigation: Implement rate limiting server-side, at the API layer, independent of and in addition to any client-side UX throttle — the server-side control is the one that actually matters for security.
Apply progressive lockout, CAPTCHA challenges, or exponential backoff on the server for repeated failed attempts on sensitive endpoints.
Ensure verification codes (OTP, reset tokens) have sufficient entropy and a short expiry window so that even a moderate rate limit makes brute-force impractical within the code's validity period.
Monitor and alert on abnormal request-volume patterns against sensitive endpoints as a compensating detective control.

links: CWE-307 (Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts)
OWASP WSTG-ATHN-03 (Testing for Weak Lock Out Mechanism)

items.title: Insecure Local Data Storage
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access. File-system search/inspection tools and, where the storage appears encoded rather than cleartext, a decompiler to identify the encoding/encryption routine in use (overlaps with the weak-local-cryptography finding where genuine encryption is attempted but poorly implemented).
items.whatItIs: The app stores sensitive data locally — cached passwords, session tokens, personal customer information, financial records, or config files containing secrets — in plain, readable text on the disk (a file, a local database, a log, or the registry) instead of encrypting it with a properly managed key.
items.rootCause: The local machine was treated as an automatically trusted place, assuming only the legitimate user could ever access their own computer. That ignores shared or multi-user machines, malware running under the same user account, lost or stolen laptops, and backup processes that might copy this data somewhere far less controlled.
items.impact: Any other local user, process or piece of malware running as the same operating system user can read the sensitive data directly. So can anyone with physical access to a lost or stolen device, or access to an unencrypted backup of the machine. None of them has to defeat the application's own login or permission checks, because the data is readable on disk.
stepsToIdentify: Use the application normally to generate representative local data (log in, perform typical business actions) while monitoring file-system and registry writes with Process Monitor.
Inspect each written location (app-data folders, local database files, log files, registry keys) directly for plaintext sensitive content — credentials, tokens, PII, business data.
For content that appears encoded rather than cleartext, attempt straightforward decoding (Base64, simple XOR) before concluding genuine encryption is in use.

Check log files and crash-dump locations specifically, since these are commonly overlooked storage locations that end up containing sensitive data logged for debugging purposes (overlaps with the crash-dump/logging-specific finding).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes local file-system/registry inspection of the test installation's data storage.
Generate representative sensitive data through normal application use.
Locate and extract the local storage locations identified during discovery.
Confirm the data is readable in plaintext (or trivially decodable) without needing the application's own credentials or any additional secret.
Document the exact file/registry paths, the type of sensitive data found, and the storage format (plaintext, weakly encoded, or genuinely but improperly encrypted).

examplePayloads.label: Monitor file/registry writes during normal application use
Search local app-data for plaintext sensitive content
Attempt straightforward decode of a suspicious stored value

variants: Sensitive data logged inadvertently to a debug/verbose log file rather than stored in the application's primary data location.

Data stored in a local SQLite/embedded database with no at-rest encryption applied at all (distinct from the embedded-database-credentials finding, which covers weak database authentication rather than storage encryption).
mitigation: Encrypt all sensitive local data at rest using a properly managed key (see the local-cryptography/key-management finding for correct key-handling guidance), not just an encoding scheme.
Minimize what sensitive data is stored locally at all — cache only what's operationally necessary, and prefer short-lived tokens over long-lived credentials or raw PII where possible.
Exclude sensitive fields from logging entirely, or mask/redact them before they're written to any log file.
Use the platform's proper credential/secret storage API (DPAPI, Keychain) for anything genuinely secret, rather than a custom local-file scheme.

links: CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File)

items.title: DLL Hijacking / Insecure Library Loading
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access. Process Monitor to trace DLL load attempts, and a means to compile or obtain a benign proof-of-concept DLL matching the expected export signature of the hijacked library.
items.whatItIs: The app (or a service/updater it installs) loads a required file (a DLL) just by its name, without specifying exactly where that file should come from. Windows then searches several folders in order to find it — some of which a regular user might be able to write to. If an attacker plants a malicious file with the right name somewhere Windows checks first, the legitimate app will load and run it — often with more privileges than the attacker had to begin with.
items.rootCause: Windows looks for a file by name across a defined list of folders, and some of those folders — the app's own directory, or a folder earlier in the system's search path — can be writable by a regular, non-admin user even when the app itself runs with elevated privileges. The app simply trusts whatever file it finds first, without checking where it actually came from or verifying its signature.
items.impact: A standard non-administrative user can plant a malicious library that the legitimate application loads and runs. If that application or a related service runs elevated, this becomes local privilege escalation. Even without elevation it is valuable to an attacker, because the code executes inside a trusted, signed process — which makes it a stealthy and reliable foothold for persistence.
stepsToIdentify: Launch the application under Process Monitor with a filter for `NAME NOT FOUND` results on `Path ends with .dll`, which reveals every DLL the application searched for but didn't find in its immediate directory — each is a hijack candidate if a writable earlier search-path location exists.

For each candidate, determine the exact search order Windows will use for that specific loading mechanism (LoadLibrary vs. LoadLibraryEx with search flags, or an app.manifest specifying a fixed search path) since this affects which directories are actually checked.
Check whether any directory earlier in the resolved search order for a candidate DLL is writable by a standard user.
Prioritize candidates loaded by an elevated service/companion process, since a hijack there yields privilege escalation rather than just same-privilege code execution.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes DLL-hijacking testing against the test installation.

Compile a proof-of-concept DLL exporting the same function signatures the legitimate DLL provides (or a minimal stub if the application doesn't immediately call into it), with a benign side effect (writing a test file, popping a message box) in DllMain.
Place the proof-of-concept DLL in the writable, earlier-in-search-order location identified during discovery.
Launch (or restart the relevant service for) the target application and confirm the proof-of-concept DLL's side effect occurs, proving it was loaded instead of the legitimate library.
If the hijacked load happens in an elevated process, confirm the proof-of-concept code executed with elevated privileges as the escalation evidence.
Remove the planted DLL after the proof-of-concept and document the exact vulnerable DLL name, search-path location, and privilege context.

examplePayloads.label: Capture DLL search misses during application launch
examplePayloads.command: procmon.exe /AcceptEula /Quiet /BackingFile dll_search_capture.pml  # filter: Path ends with .dll AND Result is NAME NOT FOUND

examplePayloads.label: Minimal proof-of-concept hijack DLL (compiled separately)
examplePayloads.command: cl /LD hijack_poc.c /Fe:version.dll  # example targeting a commonly-hijacked DLL name

examplePayloads.label: Place the proof-of-concept in the writable search-path location

variants: Phantom DLL hijacking, where the application references a DLL that doesn't exist anywhere on the system at all, making planting even simpler since there's no legitimate file to displace.
PATH-directory hijacking, where a malicious DLL is placed in a user-writable directory that appears earlier in the system/user PATH than the legitimate DLL's actual location.
mitigation: Load DLLs using a fully-qualified path or LoadLibraryEx with `LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32`/an explicit safe-directory flag, rather than an unqualified name relying on default search order.
Enable and enforce SafeDllSearchMode (default on modern Windows, but worth explicitly verifying) and avoid placing the application in a location where its working directory could be manipulated.
Sign all first-party DLLs and verify the signature before loading where the application's own loader logic permits this level of control.
Apply least-privilege file-system ACLs to the application's installation directory so standard users cannot write new files into it.
