items.title: Format String / Buffer Overflow (Native Client)
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target native (C/C++) application on a test machine you control. A fuzzing framework appropriate to the input surface (AFL++/libFuzzer for file-format or protocol fuzzing) and a debugger (WinDbg/x64dbg/GDB) with a crash-analysis extension (e.g. WinDbg's !exploitable or a GDB equivalent) to triage discovered crashes for exploitability.
items.whatItIs: The native (compiled, non-managed) app processes input it doesn't fully control — a file it opens, a network message, a command-line argument — using unsafe low-level memory operations: copying text without checking its length, indexing into an array without checking bounds, or passing user-controlled text directly into a function that expects a formatting template. This can corrupt memory and, in the worst case, let an attacker run their own code.
items.rootCause: The code performs memory operations based on the size or content of attacker-influenced input, without first checking that input against the actual size of the space set aside to hold it — or it passes attacker-controlled text as a formatting template rather than as plain data. Both are classic cases of trusting input instead of validating it before using it.
items.impact: A buffer overflow corrupts adjacent memory, including other variables, saved return addresses and function pointers. At minimum that causes a crash. Where the corruption is controllable and modern mitigations are absent or bypassed, it becomes arbitrary code execution in the vulnerable process. A format-string bug behaves similarly: it can leak memory contents, and with the right specifier it can write to memory as well.
stepsToIdentify: Identify every input surface the native application processes: file formats it opens, network protocols it parses, command-line arguments, and any embedded scripting/macro engine.
Fuzz each identified surface with a coverage-guided fuzzer (AFL++/libFuzzer) built against a debug/instrumented build of the application where source or a compatible harness is available.

For any crash produced, triage it with a crash-analysis tool to determine whether it represents a controllable memory-corruption condition (write access violation at an attacker-influenced address) versus a benign null-pointer dereference.

Separately, grep the codebase or decompiled binary for printf-family calls where the format-string argument originates from user input rather than a fixed literal, which indicates a format-string bug independent of any fuzzing campaign.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes fuzzing and crash/exploitability analysis against the test installation, and agree on effort/time budget given how open-ended fuzzing campaigns can be.
Run the fuzzer against the identified input surface for the agreed time budget, collecting and de-duplicating crashing inputs.
Triage each unique crash with the debugger's exploitability-analysis extension to prioritize genuinely controllable memory-corruption crashes over benign ones.

For a prioritized crash, attempt to demonstrate control over a key register/return address (e.g. via a cyclic pattern to determine the offset at which the instruction pointer is overwritten) as proof of the overflow's exploitability, without necessarily building a full weaponized exploit unless the engagement scope calls for it.
For any identified format-string bug, demonstrate an information-disclosure proof-of-concept (e.g. `%x` specifiers leaking stack memory) as the minimum viable evidence.
Document the exact input surface, crash signature, and assessed exploitability level (crash-only DoS vs. demonstrated control) for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Coverage-guided fuzzing of a file-parsing surface
Triage a crash for exploitability in WinDbg
Determine the exact overflow offset with a cyclic pattern
examplePayloads.command: python3 -c "from pwn import cyclic; print(cyclic(2000))" > overflow_input.txt

examplePayloads.label: Grep for user-controlled format-string usage

variants: Stack-based buffer overflow versus heap-based overflow, which require different exploitation techniques and are affected differently by modern heap-hardening mitigations.
Format-string information disclosure (read primitive) versus format-string arbitrary write (using %n-style specifiers where supported), the latter being significantly more severe.
mitigation: Use bounds-checked string/memory functions (strlcpy, snprintf with explicit size limits) throughout, and adopt a memory-safe language or a hardened C++ standard-library container usage pattern for new development where feasible.
Never pass user-controlled data directly as a printf-family format-string argument; always use a fixed format string with the user data passed as a data argument.
Enable and verify all available compiler/OS memory-protection mitigations (stack canaries, ASLR, DEP/NX, CFG) are active in release builds.
Integrate fuzzing into the regular development/CI pipeline (continuous fuzzing) rather than relying solely on periodic external VAPT engagements to catch this class of bug.

items.title: Hardcoded Secrets in Binary
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. String-extraction and decompilation tools (strings, dnSpy/ILSpy for .NET, Ghidra/IDA for native code) and, if secrets appear encoded, a scripted approach to test common encodings (Base64, hex, simple XOR) against extracted candidates.
items.whatItIs: The compiled app itself contains hardcoded secrets — API keys, database passwords, internal service tokens, encryption keys, or cloud credentials — baked directly into the code or its resource files, instead of being loaded securely at runtime from a proper secrets vault.
items.rootCause: Developers put these credentials directly into the source code during development — often just for convenience, or because there wasn't a proper secrets-management system in place — and that habit carried straight through into the shipped product. Once an app is distributed to end users, anything embedded in it can be pulled out with basic, freely available tools — there's really no such thing as a 'private' secret inside a public binary.
items.impact: An extracted credential gives the attacker whatever it unlocks — direct database access, cloud infrastructure, a third-party API, or the ability to impersonate the application to its own backend. The reach usually extends well past the machine being tested, because the same hardcoded secret ships inside every deployed copy of the application.
stepsToIdentify: Run a string-extraction pass across the full binary and all bundled resources, filtering for patterns resembling API keys, connection strings, JWT structures, or cloud-provider key formats (AWS AKIA-prefixed keys, etc.).

Decompile the application to trace any suspicious string constant back to its usage context, confirming whether it's actually used as a live credential versus an unrelated string that happens to match a pattern.
For candidates that appear encoded rather than plaintext, test straightforward decodings (Base64, hex) before concluding no secret is present.

Where a credential type is identifiable (a cloud API key, a third-party service token), attempt to validate it against that service's authentication endpoint (only with authorization, and using a read-only/benign check) to confirm it's live and current rather than a stale/revoked test value.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes extraction and, where applicable, use of any discovered hardcoded credential.
Extract candidate secrets via string extraction and decompilation as described above.
For each candidate confirmed to be a genuine, live credential, determine and document the exact scope of access it grants (which database, which cloud account/permissions, which third-party service).

Where authorized and safe to do so, perform a minimal, read-only validation of the credential's access scope (e.g. a benign authenticated API call) rather than a destructive or data-exfiltrating action.
Document every discovered secret, its type, its access scope, and whether it appears to be shared across all installations (versus somehow unique per customer/deployment).

examplePayloads.label: Broad string extraction for credential-shaped patterns
Decompile to trace a candidate string's usage
examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app.exe  # search assembly for the extracted string literal and inspect its call context

examplePayloads.label: Validate a discovered cloud key (read-only check only, with authorization)

variants: Hardcoded credential shared identically across every deployed instance of the application (highest severity, since one extraction compromises all customers) versus a credential unique to the specific tested installation.
Secret embedded in a bundled resource file (a config template, an installer script) rather than directly in the compiled binary itself.
mitigation: Remove all hardcoded secrets from source code and shipped binaries; supply credentials at runtime via a proper secrets-management solution (a vault service, environment-injected configuration) that isn't distributed to end users.

Where a client genuinely needs to call a backend service, use short-lived, narrowly-scoped tokens issued per-session/per-user rather than a single, long-lived, universally-shared credential embedded in the client.
Add automated secret-scanning (gitleaks, truffleHog, or equivalent) to the CI/CD pipeline to catch hardcoded secrets before they reach a release build.
Rotate any credential confirmed to have been exposed in a shipped binary immediately, since it must be treated as fully public once distributed.

items.title: Improper Input Validation (Thick Client)
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A fuzzing tool or manual test harness for whatever input surface is in scope (file import, form fields, command-line arguments, IPC messages), and a debugger to observe the application's behavior when malformed input is supplied.
items.whatItIs: The app accepts input — an imported file, a form field, a command-line argument, a message from another local process — without properly checking its type, length, format, or range before using it. Depending on how that unchecked input gets used later, this can cause anything from a crash to a logic error, unauthorized file access, or memory corruption.
items.rootCause: Input checking was either skipped entirely, or only applied to the 'normal' path through the app's own UI — while other ways of feeding the app input (directly editing a file, using command-line arguments, sending IPC messages) skip those same checks entirely. The assumption was that input would only ever arrive shaped exactly the way the UI itself produces it.
items.impact: Where the unchecked input ends up decides the outcome. It may only cause crashes. It may allow path traversal, reading or writing files outside the intended folder. It may reach a command or query construction point and become an injection flaw. Or it may corrupt memory in native code. Each input surface has to be traced individually rather than assumed to behave like the others.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every input surface: file-import/open dialogs, form fields, command-line arguments, configuration file values, and any IPC/network messages the application consumes.

For each surface, test with boundary and malformed values: oversized strings, unexpected data types, path-traversal sequences (`../../`), null bytes, and format-breaking characters, observing for crashes or unexpected behavior.

Trace how each input flows through the application (does it become a file path, a database query fragment, a command argument, a memory buffer size) to understand what specific vulnerability class a validation gap would enable.

Cross-reference findings against more specific, related test cases (buffer overflow, deserialization, business-logic bypass) since a general input-validation gap is often the root enabler for those more specific, higher-severity findings.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes malformed-input testing against the test installation's various input surfaces.
For each surface, systematically supply boundary/malformed values and observe application behavior (crash, error, unexpected file access, or successful unintended action).
Where a path-traversal-shaped input is accepted, attempt to read/write a file outside the application's intended working directory as proof of concept.

Where the unvalidated input flows into a downstream interpreter/query, escalate testing toward the specific relevant finding (injection, deserialization) rather than treating this as a standalone terminal finding.
Document each vulnerable input surface, the specific malformed value that triggered unexpected behavior, and the resulting impact observed.

examplePayloads.command: # supply "../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts" as the import path and observe whether it's read

examplePayloads.label: Boundary/malformed value fuzzing of a form field
Command-line argument fuzzing

variants: Path-traversal-specific input-validation gap in a file-import/export feature.
Type-confusion input-validation gap where a numeric field accepts non-numeric input that's then used unsafely in a downstream calculation or memory allocation size.
mitigation: Apply strict, allowlist-based input validation (expected type, length, character set, range) at every input surface, not just the primary UI path, and validate consistently regardless of entry point (UI, CLI, file, IPC).
Reject invalid input outright with a clear error rather than attempting to sanitize/normalize it and proceed, which is a common source of validation-bypass bugs.

Apply the principle of defense in depth: validate at the point of input AND again at the point of use (e.g. before a file-system operation constructs a path from user input), since a single validation layer can be missed or bypassed.
Include boundary and malformed-input test cases in the standard QA/regression suite rather than relying solely on periodic VAPT engagements to surface these gaps.

items.title: Insecure Auto-Update Rollback Vulnerability
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application, plus access to at least two versions of the application (a current version and a known-older, more vulnerable version) for the test machine you control. A network proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) capable of modifying the update-check/download response, and, where the update mechanism uses signed packages, tooling to inspect the signature-verification logic via decompilation.
items.whatItIs: The app's auto-update system doesn't stop you from installing an older version than what's currently running, or doesn't properly check that an update is both genuinely from the vendor and actually the latest one — not just an old version that used to be valid. This lets an attacker who can tamper with the update process force the app to reinstall a known-vulnerable older version, undoing whatever security fixes came after it.
items.rootCause: The update check confirms a package's signature is real — meaning the vendor did sign it at some point — but doesn't separately confirm the version isn't older than what's already installed. 'Genuinely signed by the vendor' and 'safe to install right now' are treated as the same thing, when they aren't — any version the vendor ever signed, including old, buggy ones, will always pass a signature check forever.
items.impact: An attacker who can intercept or modify the update channel forces the client back to a specific older version, chosen precisely because it has a known exploitable flaw. They then exploit that reintroduced vulnerability to compromise the machine. Every security fix shipped since that older version is bypassed in one move.
stepsToIdentify: Obtain a genuinely-signed older version of the application (from the vendor's own historical release archive, if available) alongside the current version.
Proxy the update-check/download flow and attempt to substitute the older, validly-signed package in place of the current update response.
Observe whether the client accepts and installs the older package without any version-currency check, or whether it correctly detects and rejects the downgrade attempt.

Where the update mechanism relies on an update-manifest/metadata file separate from the package itself, check whether that manifest's own integrity/authenticity (and its stated version number) is independently verified, since manipulating the manifest alone (without needing a fake package) may be sufficient.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes update-mechanism manipulation testing against the test installation, and obtain a legitimately-signed older version with a documented, known vulnerability for use as the downgrade target.
Proxy the application's update-check request and substitute a response pointing to (or directly serve) the older, validly-signed package.
Trigger the client's update process and confirm whether the older version installs successfully.

If the downgrade succeeds, demonstrate exploitation of the specific known vulnerability present in that older version as the full impact chain, tying the update-mechanism weakness to a concrete, exploitable outcome.
Document the exact update-check/verification logic gap (missing version-currency check, unauthenticated manifest) and the specific downgrade-enabled vulnerability chained.

examplePayloads.label: Intercept and modify the update-check response
examplePayloads.command: # Burp: intercept the update-manifest response, rewrite version field and download URL to point at the older signed package

examplePayloads.label: Serve a substituted older package directly
Decompile to inspect the update-verification logic for a version-currency check
examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app.exe  # search Updater module for version-comparison logic alongside the signature-check call

variants: Unauthenticated update manifest, where only the package itself is signed but the manifest specifying which version/URL to fetch is not, allowing manifest tampering alone to redirect to an older package.

Signature check present and version-currency check present, but the version-comparison logic itself is flawed (e.g. simple string comparison rather than proper semantic version comparison, allowing a crafted version string to be misread as newer).
mitigation: Enforce a strict monotonic version check as part of update installation, independent of and in addition to signature verification — reject any package whose version is not strictly greater than the currently-installed version (absent an explicit, deliberate, separately-authorized downgrade flow).
Sign and independently verify the update manifest/metadata itself, not just the final package, so manifest tampering alone cannot redirect the client to an older or malicious package.

Maintain a server-side revocation list of known-vulnerable historical versions and have the client check against it (or rely on the monotonic-version enforcement above) so those versions can never be reinstalled even with a valid signature.
Use a well-tested semantic-version comparison library rather than custom string-comparison logic for the version-currency check.

items.title: Insecure Command-Line Argument Passing of Secrets
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access shared with (or accessible to) another local account for demonstrating cross-user visibility. Process Explorer/Task Manager (with the Command Line column enabled) or `wmic process get commandline` for process-list inspection.
items.whatItIs: The app (or a helper program it launches) passes a sensitive value — a password, an API token, a session secret — directly as a plain, visible command-line argument when starting another process, instead of using something more private like an environment variable or a temporary file. On most operating systems, any other user or process on the machine can see the full command line — arguments included — of anything currently running.
items.rootCause: Passing values as command-line arguments is the simplest way to hand data to a new process. What was never weighed is the sensitivity of that specific value against how visible command-line arguments actually are. They are treated as private, when in reality any other local process can read them just by listing what is running.
items.impact: Any other user on the machine, or any lower-privileged process able to list running processes, can read the secret straight from the process list. No special privilege is needed, because listing processes and their command lines is available to standard users on most default operating system configurations.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger the application to spawn the relevant child process/helper script (e.g. during login, an update check, or a specific feature invocation) while monitoring process creation with Process Monitor or Process Explorer.

Inspect the full command line of the spawned process (enabling the Command Line column in Process Explorer, or via `wmic process get commandline` / `ps aux` on Unix-like systems) for any sensitive-looking values.

From a second, separate local user account (or a low-privileged background process), confirm the same command-line argument is visible, demonstrating the cross-user/cross-process exposure rather than assuming it based on same-user observation alone.
Check whether the same secret is also exposed in shell history, system/application event logs, or process-accounting logs that record command lines.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes process-list inspection during normal application operation on the test installation.
Trigger the application action that spawns the process carrying the sensitive command-line argument.
From a second local user account (or a low-privileged monitoring process), enumerate running processes and extract the exposed secret from the command line.
Demonstrate use of the extracted secret (e.g. authenticate to the associated service/API) as proof of real-world impact, if safely and appropriately scoped to do so.
Document the exact process, argument, and the extraction method (which user/privilege level was sufficient to observe it).

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate running processes with full command lines (Windows)
Enumerate running processes with full command lines (Unix-like)
Continuous monitoring for a short-lived spawned process carrying a secret
examplePayloads.command: while ($true) { Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select CommandLine | Out-File -Append cmdline_log.txt; Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 200 }

variants: Secret exposed in a short-lived helper process that exits quickly, requiring continuous/rapid process-list polling to catch, versus a long-running process where the exposure window is effectively indefinite.
Secret additionally persisted in shell history or an event/process-accounting log, extending the exposure window well beyond the process's actual runtime.
mitigation: Pass sensitive values to spawned processes via a secure channel not visible in the process list: an inherited handle/pipe, a temporary file with restrictive permissions deleted immediately after use, standard input, or an environment variable scoped narrowly (noting some platforms also expose environment variables to sufficiently privileged inspectors, so this is a partial improvement, not a complete fix).
Where feasible, have the child process retrieve the secret itself from a proper secret store rather than receiving it from the parent at all.
Audit all inter-process secret-passing mechanisms in the application for this pattern, since it's easy to overlook in helper scripts and updater/installer components specifically.
Ensure no logging subsystem (application, OS, or shell history) inadvertently persists command lines containing secrets.

links: CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor)

items.title: Insecure Handling of Clipboard Data Containing Secrets
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A clipboard-monitoring utility or a simple script polling the OS clipboard API, run from a second application/process context to demonstrate cross-application visibility.
items.whatItIs: A 'copy to clipboard' button copies sensitive data — a password, an API key, a one-time code, a full card number — to the system clipboard, and never clears it afterward, and doesn't use any 'exclude from clipboard history' option the OS might offer. That means any other app on the machine that can read the clipboard can grab that secret for as long as it stays there.
items.rootCause: The clipboard is a shared, unauthenticated resource on basically every desktop and mobile OS — any app with basic clipboard access (which is usually unrestricted) can read whatever was last copied there. This convenience feature was built without accounting for that shared access, and without using the auto-clear or exclusion options meant to reduce exactly this risk.
items.impact: Any other application on the machine can silently read the value while it sits on the clipboard, including malware, a browser extension, or an ordinary installed program with clipboard access. On platforms with a clipboard history feature the value can persist well beyond the moment it was copied, extending the exposure window further.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger the application's copy-to-clipboard feature for a sensitive value (a password reveal-and-copy button, an OTP code, a payment card number).
From a separate, independent application/process, poll the clipboard immediately after the copy operation and confirm the sensitive value is readable.

Measure how long the value remains on the clipboard before (if ever) the application clears it, and compare against reasonable practice (a short timeout, typically 30-60 seconds, is the common mitigation).

Check whether the platform's clipboard-history feature (Windows Clipboard History, for example) retains the value even after the application's own clear/timeout, and whether the application used the appropriate API flag to exclude itself from that history.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes clipboard-monitoring testing against the test installation.
Trigger the copy-to-clipboard action for a sensitive value within the application.
From a separate monitoring process/script, capture the clipboard content immediately and confirm the sensitive value is present.
If applicable, check the OS clipboard-history feature for continued presence of the value after the application's own session ends.
Document the exact sensitive data type exposed, the duration it remained accessible, and whether clipboard-history persistence extended that exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Monitor clipboard content from a separate process (PowerShell)
Monitor clipboard content (Linux, X11)
Check Windows Clipboard History retention after the app's own session ends
examplePayloads.command: # open Win+V clipboard history UI and check whether the copied sensitive value is still listed

variants: Sensitive value persisted in OS-level clipboard history (a longer-lived, separate exposure) versus only the immediate, single-slot clipboard buffer.
Sensitive value copied automatically (without explicit user action) as a side effect of another feature, increasing the chance of inadvertent exposure.
mitigation: Clear the clipboard automatically a short, fixed time after copying a sensitive value (commonly 30-60 seconds), and clear it immediately if the application is closed or loses focus before that timeout.

Use the platform's "sensitive data" clipboard API flag where available (e.g. Windows' CF_EXCLUDECLIPBOARDCONTENTFROMMONITORPROCESSING / excluding from Clipboard History) to prevent history persistence.
Minimize reliance on clipboard-based convenience features for highly sensitive values; where feasible, offer a masked, in-app "reveal" instead of a full clipboard copy.
Educate users, where the copy-to-clipboard feature is retained, that clipboard contents are shared system-wide and should be treated as temporarily exposed.

links: OWASP MASVS-STORAGE (clipboard-handling guidance, applicable analogously to desktop clients)

items.title: Insecure Inter-Process Communication
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application and its companion process(es)/service on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access. Sysinternals Process Explorer/WinObj to enumerate named pipes/mailslots/shared memory objects, and their permissions, plus a means to construct and send arbitrary messages on the discovered channel.
items.whatItIs: Different parts of the app — the main window, a background service, a helper process — communicate over a local channel such as a named pipe, shared memory, or a local socket. That channel either does not verify who is connecting at all, or has permissions loose enough that any regular local program can connect and send messages to it, not only the app's own components.
items.rootCause: These communication channels were built assuming only the app's own pieces would ever use them, without adding any access restriction (locking the channel down to the specific expected program) or authentication (a shared secret proving the sender is legitimate) to actually enforce that assumption.
items.impact: Any other local process can connect to the channel, including malware or something running under attacker control. At minimum they eavesdrop on the data passing over it. More seriously, they can send forged messages that the receiving component acts on. Where that component runs elevated, this becomes a route to local privilege escalation rather than just unintended behaviour.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the application's IPC surface: named pipes, mailslots, and shared-memory/mapped-file objects, using WinObj or a similar object-namespace browser (or `lsof`/`ls /tmp` equivalents for Unix domain sockets).
Check the DACL/permissions on each discovered IPC object for standard-user connect/write access using accesschk.
For channels found to be connectable by a standard user, capture legitimate traffic on the channel (where possible) to understand its message format.
Determine which component is on the receiving end of each channel and its privilege level, prioritizing channels feeding into an elevated process as higher severity.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes IPC-channel connection and message-injection testing against the test installation.
Connect to the identified IPC object as a standard user/independent process, confirming the connection succeeds without any authentication challenge.
Capture or infer the expected message format, then construct and send a forged message to the channel.
Observe the receiving component's behavior for evidence that the forged message was accepted and acted upon (a UI state change, a file written, a privileged action performed).
If the receiving component runs elevated, demonstrate the resulting privilege-escalation impact as the most severe evidence for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate named pipes and their permissions
Connect to and send data on a discovered named pipe
examplePayloads.command: python3 -c "import win32pipe, win32file; h = win32file.CreateFile(r'\\.\pipe\<PipeName>', win32file.GENERIC_WRITE, 0, None, win32file.OPEN_EXISTING, 0, None); win32file.WriteFile(h, b'<forged-message>')"

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate Unix domain sockets (Linux/macOS equivalent)

variants: IPC channel feeding into an elevated (SYSTEM/root) receiving process, providing a local privilege-escalation path rather than just same-privilege message injection.
IPC channel carrying sensitive data readable by eavesdropping alone, without needing to inject forged messages at all.
mitigation: Restrict IPC object DACLs (named pipe/shared-memory permissions) to only the specific, expected process/service account, denying connect/write access to standard users or Everyone/Authenticated Users groups.

Authenticate the calling process at the application level in addition to OS-level object permissions — verify the sender's identity/integrity (e.g. via a signed message or a mutually-derived session token) rather than trusting any connection that reaches the channel.
Validate and sanity-check all messages received over IPC as untrusted input, regardless of the sending process's assumed identity.

Where the receiving component is privileged, apply the same least-privilege design principle as the general privilege-escalation findings: minimize what a single IPC message can cause the privileged component to do.

items.title: Insecure Network Communication
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A network intercepting proxy or packet capture tool (Wireshark, Burp Suite/mitmproxy) positioned to observe the application's network traffic to its backend.
items.whatItIs: The app talks to its server (or a local companion service) over a connection that's completely unencrypted (plain HTTP or a raw network connection with no TLS), or only partly encrypted — some features use HTTPS while others, like a telemetry check-in or license verification, don't. Whatever travels over that unencrypted part is visible to anyone watching the network.
items.rootCause: Not every feature that talks over the network got covered by the same 'always use encryption' standard applied to the app's main functionality. Secondary features — update checks, analytics, license pings — often get added later in development and slip past the security review that covered the primary traffic.
items.impact: Anyone on the network path can read the unencrypted traffic — on shared or public Wi-Fi, through a compromised router, or by positioning themselves on the local segment. Where that traffic carries credentials, session tokens or business data, it becomes credential theft or session hijacking. And since the channel has no integrity protection either, they can modify responses rather than only observing them.
stepsToIdentify: Capture the application's full network traffic during a comprehensive walkthrough of its features (login, primary functionality, settings, update check, any telemetry/analytics call) using Wireshark or a proxy configured to intercept all traffic, not just HTTP(S).
Filter the capture for any traffic on standard unencrypted ports (80, 23, a custom unencrypted port) or any TLS handshake that fails/downgrades unexpectedly.
For each unencrypted channel found, identify what data it carries — flag any credential, token, or sensitive business data specifically.
Cross-reference against the certificate-pinning finding, since a channel that does use TLS but without pinning is a related but distinct issue from one using no encryption at all.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes network traffic capture during a full feature walkthrough of the test installation.
Capture traffic across every feature of the application, including secondary/background channels (update checks, telemetry) not just the primary login/business-function flow.
Identify and extract any sensitive data (credentials, tokens, PII, business data) observed in cleartext.
Where credentials/tokens are captured, attempt to use them against the corresponding service as proof-of-impact evidence, using only test accounts.
Document every unencrypted channel found, the data it exposed, and its business purpose (primary function vs. a secondary/overlooked feature).

examplePayloads.label: Full-traffic capture during a feature walkthrough
examplePayloads.command: tshark -i eth0 -w full_app_traffic.pcap  # perform login, core feature use, settings, update-check while capturing

examplePayloads.label: Filter capture for cleartext HTTP traffic specifically
Extract cleartext credentials from a captured HTTP POST

variants: Primary application functionality correctly using TLS while a secondary channel (telemetry, licensing check, crash reporting) uses plain HTTP.
TLS used but silently downgrading to plaintext on connection failure rather than failing closed, which an active attacker can force by blocking the TLS handshake.
mitigation: Enforce TLS for every network-communicating feature of the application, including secondary/background channels, with no plaintext fallback under any failure condition (fail closed, not open).
Apply certificate pinning (see the related finding) in addition to basic TLS to protect against a MITM presenting an otherwise-trusted certificate.
Conduct a full-traffic-capture review (as used in this identification process) as a standing pre-release check, specifically to catch overlooked secondary channels.
Disable or remove legacy, unencrypted protocol support entirely rather than leaving it available as a fallback.

items.title: Lack of Binary Protection (No Obfuscation/Anti-Tamper)
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A disassembler/decompiler (Ghidra, IDA, dnSpy/ILSpy) and a debugger (x64dbg) to assess how readily the binary yields to standard static and dynamic analysis.
items.whatItIs: The app ships with no tamper protection, no code obfuscation, and no self-check for integrity at all. It's a straightforward build that decompiles almost back to readable source code, has nothing stopping a debugger from attaching to it, and never verifies its own code hasn't been modified while running or after installation.
items.rootCause: Binary protection just wasn't part of the release process — either the team didn't consider reverse-engineering resistance necessary for this particular product, or it was deprioritized in favor of shipping features faster. The result is a compiled app that's exactly as easy to analyze and modify as a raw development build.
items.impact: The absence of binary protection lowers the effort for every other client-side attack in this domain — tampering with business logic, bypassing licence checks, extracting hardcoded secrets, hooking functions at runtime. None of them has to defeat an anti-tampering layer first, because there isn't one. Read this as a multiplier on the other findings rather than something exploitable on its own.
stepsToIdentify: Attempt straightforward decompilation of the binary and assess how close the output is to readable, near-original source code (trivial for unobfuscated .NET/Java bytecode, more involved but still very feasible for unobfuscated native code).
Attempt to attach a standard debugger to a running instance and confirm no anti-debugging countermeasure triggers.
Check whether the binary performs any self-integrity check (a checksum/hash of its own code segments compared against an expected value) at startup, by searching decompiled code for such a routine.
Assess whether any commercial or open-source packer/obfuscator/protector is applied at all (even weak, defeatable protection is a materially different finding than none whatsoever).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes static/dynamic analysis of the test installation's binary.
Decompile the binary and demonstrate the ease of obtaining readable logic for a security-sensitive routine (a license check, a crypto function) as evidence.
Attach a debugger and confirm unhindered ability to set breakpoints, step through execution, and modify memory/registers at will.

Where feasible within the engagement's scope, chain this finding into a concrete demonstration of one of the other client-side findings (a business-logic bypass or hooking demonstration) to show the practical consequence of the missing protection, rather than reporting it as a purely theoretical gap.

Recommend layered protection (commercial obfuscator/packer plus a genuine anti-tamper/self-integrity check) rather than relying on any single technique, since a determined attacker with static+dynamic analysis tooling can usually defeat one layer alone.

examplePayloads.label: Assess decompilation readability
examplePayloads.command: dnSpy target_app.exe  # or Ghidra for native binaries — check whether logic is fully readable without significant manual reconstruction

examplePayloads.label: Confirm unhindered debugger attachment
examplePayloads.command: x64dbg target_app.exe  # attach and set a breakpoint on a security-relevant function without any anti-debug trigger

examplePayloads.label: Search for (absence of) a self-integrity-check routine

variants: Complete absence of any protection versus weak/outdated protection (an old, publicly-defeated packer or an easily-bypassed anti-debug check) that provides negligible real-world resistance despite technically being present.

Anti-tamper checks (integrity self-verification, debugger detection) implemented but only client-side and easily patched out with a binary edit, versus checks that also report to a server-side verification endpoint the attacker cannot silence purely by modifying the local binary.
mitigation: Apply a reputable commercial or well-maintained open-source obfuscation/protection solution appropriate to the runtime, understanding this raises attacker effort rather than providing an absolute guarantee.
Implement runtime self-integrity verification (checksumming critical code segments at startup and periodically during execution) and anti-debugging countermeasures as defense in depth.
Prioritize moving genuinely security-critical logic server-side (see the client-side-trust-boundary finding) rather than relying on binary protection alone to safeguard client-resident logic.
Treat binary protection as one layer in a defense-in-depth strategy, not a substitute for proper server-side enforcement of anything with real security or financial consequence.

items.title: Sensitive Data Exposure in Crash Dumps/Logs
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A means to trigger an application crash (an invalid input, a debugger-forced exception) and access to wherever crash dumps or verbose logs are written (a local folder, or a remote crash-reporting/telemetry backend if the application uploads dumps automatically).
items.whatItIs: When the app crashes or writes detailed diagnostic logs, the resulting report contains whatever sensitive data happened to be in memory or in the log context at that moment. That can include passwords, session tokens, encryption keys or confidential business data. It happens because the logging or crash-reporting tool captures a broad snapshot without first removing known-sensitive fields.
items.rootCause: Crash reporting and detailed logging are designed to capture as much context as possible, which is genuinely useful for debugging. What is missing is a step stripping sensitive fields before that dump or log is written to disk. In many products it is also uploaded automatically to the vendor's own crash-reporting service.
items.impact: Anyone with access to the crash dump or log file can extract sensitive data that was never meant to leave the running application's memory. That includes another local user, any process with file-system read access, and — where dumps upload automatically — anyone who can reach the vendor's crash-reporting backend, which is a much wider group than the machine's own users.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger a crash or enable verbose logging while the application holds representative sensitive data in memory (logged in, mid-transaction) and inspect the resulting dump/log file directly for plaintext sensitive content.
Check whether crash dumps are automatically uploaded to a vendor backend, and if so, whether that upload occurs over an encrypted channel and to an access-controlled destination.

Review log-level configuration to determine whether verbose/debug logging (which is more likely to capture full request/response bodies including secrets) can be enabled in production, either by the user or by default.
Cross-reference with the general insecure-local-data-storage finding, since crash dumps/logs are a specific, commonly-overlooked storage location within that broader class.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes crash-inducing and log-inspection testing against the test installation.
Populate the application with representative sensitive test data (login, perform a sensitive transaction) then trigger a crash or enable verbose logging for the relevant operation.
Locate and inspect the resulting crash dump/log file for plaintext sensitive content.

If auto-upload to a vendor backend is confirmed, document the transmission channel's security (encrypted/unencrypted) as an additional exposure dimension, without needing direct access to the vendor's backend itself.
Document the exact sensitive data types found and the file's default access permissions/location.

examplePayloads.command: # supply a malformed value known to trigger an unhandled exception during a session where test credentials/tokens are active

examplePayloads.label: Search a generated crash dump for sensitive strings
Enable and inspect verbose application logging
examplePayloads.command: # set log level to Debug/Verbose via config, reproduce a sensitive action, then grep the resulting log file

variants: Sensitive data captured in a locally-stored crash dump only, versus a dump that's automatically uploaded to a vendor telemetry/crash-reporting backend, which extends exposure beyond the local machine.
Sensitive data present in verbose/debug-level application logs even without any crash occurring at all.
mitigation: Implement redaction/scrubbing of known-sensitive fields (passwords, tokens, keys, PII patterns) before writing any crash dump or log entry.
Restrict crash-dump and log-file permissions to the owning user/administrators only, and apply the same access controls to any local staging location before upload.
Encrypt crash dumps/logs in transit if automatically uploaded to a vendor backend, and apply strict access control on that backend.
Default to a conservative (non-verbose) logging level in production builds, requiring an explicit, audited action to enable verbose logging temporarily for diagnostic purposes.

items.title: Sensitive Data in Memory
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control, with standard (non-administrative) user access sufficient to read the process's own memory, or administrative access if using a full memory-dumping tool. A memory-forensics tool (Process Hacker's memory-string search, WinDbg, or a dedicated tool like Mimikatz for credential-specific memory scraping where applicable) to search live process memory for sensitive content.
items.whatItIs: Sensitive data — passwords, decrypted tokens, encryption keys, confidential business data — stays sitting in the app's memory in plain, readable form for longer than it actually needs to, instead of being cleared right after use. In some cases this happens because the programming language's string type simply can't be reliably wiped from memory, even if the app tries to clear it. That means the data can be recovered later by inspecting the process's memory, or from a crash dump, well after it was actually needed.
items.rootCause: Sensitive values are often stored using the language's standard, unchangeable string type (like .NET's String or Python's str), which — once created — can't reliably be overwritten in memory before the system eventually cleans it up on its own schedule. Combined with no deliberate effort to clear genuinely sensitive values immediately after use, secrets end up lingering in memory far longer than they should.
items.impact: Anyone able to read the application's process memory can recover secrets the application logic considered finished with. That includes a local attacker with sufficient privilege, malware running in the same context, or someone holding a memory or crash dump of the process. The practical exposure window for those secrets ends up far longer than their intended momentary use.
stepsToIdentify: Use the application to process representative sensitive data (log in, decrypt a protected value, perform a transaction requiring a key).

Immediately after the operation completes (well past when the value should logically still be needed), take a memory snapshot/dump of the running process and search it for the plaintext sensitive value.
Repeat after progressively longer delays to characterize how long the value persists in memory before being overwritten/garbage-collected naturally.

Identify, via decompilation, whether the code uses an immutable string type for the sensitive value (a strong indicator this finding applies) versus a mutable byte buffer that's explicitly zeroed after use.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes process-memory inspection of the test installation.
Trigger the application to process representative sensitive test data.
Capture a memory dump of the running process shortly after the operation completes.
Search the dump for the plaintext sensitive value using a string-search or memory-forensics tool.
Document how long after logical "use" the value remained recoverable, and whether the code's use of an immutable string type versus a properly-zeroed buffer explains the persistence.

examplePayloads.label: Dump the target process's memory for inspection
Search the dump for a known sensitive test value
Live memory string search without a full dump (Process Hacker)
examplePayloads.command: # Process Hacker: right-click process -> Properties -> Memory -> Strings, filter for known sensitive test value

variants: Encryption keys persisting in memory well after the encryption/decryption operation completes, distinct from password/token persistence.
Sensitive data recoverable from a hibernation file or page file (swapped-out memory) even after the process itself has exited, extending exposure beyond the process's own runtime.
mitigation: Use mutable, explicitly-zeroable byte buffers (e.g. `SecureString` where genuinely still appropriate for the platform, or a custom pinned byte array) for sensitive values instead of standard immutable string types, and zero them immediately after use.
Minimize the lifetime and number of copies of any sensitive value in memory — avoid unnecessary string concatenation/manipulation that creates additional, uncontrolled copies.
Where the platform supports it, use OS-level protected-memory APIs (e.g. Windows CryptProtectMemory) for particularly sensitive material like encryption keys.
Disable or encrypt the system page/swap file and hibernation file on machines handling particularly sensitive data, as a compensating control against memory contents being written to disk.

items.title: Unvalidated Update Mechanism
items.prerequisites: A local installation of the target application on a test machine you control. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) capable of modifying the update-check response and serving a substitute package, and a benign proof-of-concept executable to serve as the malicious "update."
items.whatItIs: The app's auto-updater downloads and runs update files without properly verifying a real cryptographic signature — or checks something so weak (like a simple checksum an attacker can also just recalculate to match their own fake file) that it doesn't actually prove anything. Anyone who can influence the update process — by sitting in the middle of the network connection or compromising the download server — can deliver their own malicious file and have it run with the same trust and privilege as a real update.
items.rootCause: The updater was built to just download and run whatever file it finds at the expected location, without an independent check that only the real vendor (holding a private signing key the attacker doesn't have) could have produced. A checksum alone doesn't prove anything — if someone swaps the file, they can just as easily recompute a matching checksum for their fake one.
items.impact: This is complete compromise of any machine running the vulnerable updater. An attacker who can intercept or redirect the update channel delivers arbitrary code, and it runs with whatever privilege the update process holds — often elevated, since installing updates usually requires administrative rights. Given how much trust and reach an update mechanism carries, this is among the most severe findings possible in this domain.
stepsToIdentify: Capture the application's update-check and package-download traffic via a proxy to identify the exact request/response flow and whether it occurs over TLS.
Determine what integrity mechanism (if any) is applied to the downloaded package: a cryptographic signature verified against an embedded public key, a simple checksum, or no verification at all.
If only a checksum is used, confirm it's genuinely insufficient by substituting an alternate file and recomputing a matching checksum, then checking whether the client accepts it.
If a signature check exists, assess its robustness (does it verify against a properly pinned, non-user-writable public key, or could the trust anchor itself be tampered with locally).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes update-channel interception and substitute-package delivery testing against the test installation.
Prepare a benign proof-of-concept executable (a harmless action such as writing a test file or popping a message box) to serve as the substitute "update."

Intercept the update-check/download flow via the proxy and substitute the benign proof-of-concept in place of the legitimate package, adjusting any checksum field in the response to match if that's the only check present.
Trigger the client's update installation process and confirm whether the substituted package executes.
Document the exact integrity-verification gap (none, checksum-only, or a bypassable signature check) and the resulting privilege level the substituted code executed at.

examplePayloads.label: Intercept the update-check response and substitute the package URL/checksum
examplePayloads.command: # Burp: modify the update manifest response to point at an attacker-hosted URL, recompute and substitute a matching checksum if that's the only integrity field checked

examplePayloads.label: Serve the substitute (benign proof-of-concept) package
Confirm execution and privilege level of the substituted package
examplePayloads.command: # observe Task Manager/Process Explorer for the executed proof-of-concept process and its run-as account

variants: No integrity check at all versus a checksum-only check that provides the illusion of protection without any real cryptographic guarantee.
Signature check present but the embedded/trusted public key or CA is itself stored in a user-writable location, allowing local tampering with the trust anchor even without a network MITM position.
mitigation: Sign all update packages with a private key held exclusively by the vendor, and verify that signature client-side against a public key embedded in (and not independently modifiable within) the application.
Serve updates exclusively over TLS with certificate pinning, in addition to package-level signature verification, as defense in depth against both channel-level and package-level tampering.

Ensure the trust anchor (embedded public key/certificate) cannot be overwritten by a standard local user, since a locally-tamperable trust anchor undermines even a correctly-implemented signature check.

Treat the update mechanism as the single highest-value target in the entire thick-client attack surface during design review, given its inherent broad reach and typically elevated execution privilege.

items.title: Electron / Web-Hybrid Desktop Application Node Integration Abuse
items.prerequisites: An installed Electron, NW.js, Tauri or similar web-hybrid desktop application. Ability to unpack the application archive (the app.asar bundle in Electron's case) and read its JavaScript. Access to the app's developer tools where enabled, or a means of injecting content into any window it renders. Authorisation covering local binary modification, since testing involves unpacking and potentially repacking application resources.
items.whatItIs: An Electron-style application is a bundled web app running in a stripped-down browser, but with one decisive difference: its JavaScript may be granted access to the operating system — filesystem, process spawning, native modules. Whether it is depends on three settings per window: whether Node integration is enabled, whether context isolation is on, and whether the sandbox is enabled. If a window renders any content an attacker can influence while Node integration is on and isolation is off, a cross-site scripting flaw stops being a browser-scoped bug and becomes command execution on the host.
items.rootCause: Node integration exists because it makes development straightforward — the UI code can simply call filesystem and process APIs directly. Disabling it and routing privileged operations through a narrow, explicitly-defined preload bridge is more work, so applications frequently ship with the permissive configuration retained from early development. Compounding this, developers apply browser-era assumptions about XSS severity to a context where the browser's sandbox has been deliberately removed, and the risk is judged as if it were an ordinary web page.
items.impact: Any content injection in a Node-enabled window yields arbitrary code execution with the logged-in user's privileges — reading and writing files, spawning processes, establishing persistence, and reaching internal network resources from a trusted endpoint. The injection source need not be exotic: a chat message, a rendered document, a fetched remote page, or a crafted deep link is enough. Because the application is a signed, trusted desktop binary, the resulting activity is attributed to it rather than to obviously malicious software, and endpoint controls frequently permit it on that basis.
stepsToIdentify: Unpack the application bundle and locate the main process source, which is where each window's security options are set.
For every window the app creates, record whether nodeIntegration is enabled, contextIsolation is disabled, and sandbox is off — the dangerous combination is Node on with isolation off.
Inspect any preload script for functions exposed to the renderer, since an over-broad bridge reintroduces the same risk even when Node integration is correctly disabled.
Determine whether the app loads any remote content, renders user-supplied HTML or Markdown, or opens links in an app window rather than the system browser — each is a candidate injection point.
Check whether a Content-Security-Policy is applied to app windows, and whether webSecurity has been explicitly disabled anywhere.
Check the registered custom protocol handlers, since deep links are a common way to reach app functionality from outside and are frequently parsed without validation.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers local binary unpacking and code execution on the test host, and work on a snapshot-capable VM you can restore.
Prove the configuration first by reading the window options directly from the unpacked source — this establishes the finding without executing anything.
Where an injection point is confirmed, demonstrate reach with a benign, clearly-marked action such as writing a distinctly named file to a temporary directory.
Do not escalate to a full payload; showing that the Node API is reachable from renderer context is sufficient to establish severity.
Where a preload bridge is present, enumerate exactly which functions it exposes and test whether any accepts a path or command argument without validation.
Report the specific window and its exact option set, since the fix is a per-window configuration change rather than a general hardening exercise, and remove any test artefacts afterwards.

examplePayloads.label: Unpack the application bundle
Locate window security options
Detect the dangerous combination
Benign reachability proof from renderer context
Inspect the preload bridge surface
Enumerate registered deep-link handlers

variants: Preload-bridge abuse where Node integration is correctly disabled but the exposed bridge passes attacker-controlled arguments into a privileged operation.
Deep-link injection where a custom protocol handler parses an attacker-supplied URL and routes it into an app window without validation.
Outdated framework version carrying a known renderer escape, which defeats an otherwise-correct configuration.
Disabled webSecurity on a window, permitting cross-origin reads that reintroduce a class of attack the browser would normally prevent.
mitigation: Disable nodeIntegration and enable contextIsolation and sandbox on every window — this is the single change that reduces a renderer compromise back to browser scope.
Expose privileged operations only through a narrow, explicitly-defined preload bridge with validated arguments, never a general-purpose passthrough.
Apply a strict Content-Security-Policy to app windows and never disable webSecurity.
Open external links in the system browser rather than an application window, so remote content never renders in a privileged context.
Validate deep-link input as untrusted, exactly as a web application would treat a request parameter.
Keep the framework version current, since renderer escapes are patched upstream and an outdated runtime undermines correct configuration.

items.title: Custom URI Protocol Handler Argument Injection
items.prerequisites: A desktop application that registers a custom URI scheme, which most installed clients do for deep linking and single sign-on callbacks. Access to a workstation with the application installed. The ability to get the user to visit a web page or open a document, since a registered scheme can be invoked from a browser. Registry or launch services access is useful for reading the registered command template.
items.whatItIs: Registering a scheme means the operating system will launch the application with attacker-supplied text whenever a page uses that scheme. The registered command is usually a template with the URI substituted into it, and if that substitution lands in a shell context or in a position where it can be read as another flag, the URI stops being data and becomes part of the command line. The attacker never needs to run code directly — the browser hands the string to the operating system, which hands it to the application.
items.rootCause: The registered command template is written once at install time and treated as a fixed string rather than as a place where untrusted input arrives. Applications commonly parse the URI with string splitting instead of a URI parser, so encoded separators and quotes survive. Browsers prompt before invoking an external handler, but the prompt names the application rather than showing the arguments, so the user is approving something they cannot see.
items.impact: Depending on how the application consumes the argument, the outcome ranges from forcing the client into a debug or insecure mode, to pointing it at an attacker-controlled server, to command execution where the template passes through a shell. Because the user only sees a prompt asking whether to open a familiar application, the interaction looks routine. The attack works from any web page, so no prior access to the workstation is needed.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the URI schemes the application registers, from the registry on Windows or the application bundle on macOS.
Read the registered command template and note exactly where the URI is substituted and whether it is quoted.
Determine whether the template invokes the binary directly or routes through a shell or script interpreter.
Review how the application parses the received URI: a real parser, or string splitting on separators.
Identify which command-line flags the application accepts, since injecting a flag is often easier than injecting a command.
Test whether encoded characters survive the browser, the operating system and the application's own parsing.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers local execution on the test workstation and agree what may be launched.
Invoke the scheme with a benign value and confirm the application launches, establishing the baseline path.
Append an additional argument after a separator and observe whether the application treats it as a flag rather than as part of the URI.
Where the template is unquoted, test whether a space-separated value splits into two arguments.
Try flags with observable effects first, such as a logging or configuration override, before anything heavier.
Demonstrate delivery from a web page rather than a terminal, since that is the realistic path and it changes the severity.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate registered schemes (Windows)
examplePayloads.command: reg query HKCR /f "URL Protocol" /s | findstr /i HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT

examplePayloads.label: Read the command template
Enumerate handlers (macOS)

Unquoted template split
Delivery from a page

variants: A scheme registered by an installed browser extension or helper rather than the main application.
Argument injection through a file association instead of a URI scheme, triggered by opening a document.
A single sign-on callback scheme where the injected argument redirects the token to an attacker endpoint.
Scheme hijacking, where a second application registers the same scheme and receives the deep links intended for the first.
mitigation: Quote the substitution point in the registered command template, and never route it through a shell or script interpreter.
Parse the received URI with a proper parser and validate it against an expected structure before use.
Treat everything after the scheme as untrusted data that can never become a command-line flag, for example by passing it on a separate channel after launch.
Reject URIs containing separators, quotes or flag prefixes rather than attempting to sanitise them.
Restrict which application actions a deep link can reach, excluding debug, configuration and update functions entirely.
Where the scheme is used for authentication callbacks, bind the callback to a state value issued at request time so an injected callback is rejected.

items.title: Exposed Localhost HTTP API Surface in Desktop Clients
items.prerequisites: A desktop application that runs a local HTTP or WebSocket listener, which is common for clients with browser extensions, hardware integrations, or a web-technology user interface. Access to a workstation with the application running. A browser for testing cross-origin reachability, since any visited page can attempt requests to localhost.
items.whatItIs: A local listener feels private because it binds to the loopback address, but any web page the user visits can send requests to it. The browser's same-origin policy restricts reading responses, not sending requests, and many of these listeners either allow all origins outright or accept simple requests that need no preflight. So a page on an unrelated site can reach an API that the developer assumed only their own components would call.
items.rootCause: The listener is built for internal communication between the application's own parts, so authentication is often omitted entirely on the reasoning that only local software can reach it. Permissive cross-origin headers are frequently added during development to make a browser extension work and never tightened. Where a token is used, it is commonly a fixed value stored in a world-readable configuration file, which any local process can read.
items.impact: What an attacker gains depends on what the API exposes, and these interfaces are usually privileged because they were meant to be internal: reading local files, triggering updates, retrieving stored credentials, or executing application functions. Reachability from any visited web page turns a local interface into a remote attack surface with no user interaction beyond browsing. Any other local process can reach it too, which breaks the boundary between a standard user and the application's privileges.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate listening sockets while the application runs and identify which belong to it, including ports opened only after certain features are used.
Determine whether each listener binds to loopback only or to all interfaces, since the latter makes it network-reachable.
Probe the listener for a routing surface: common paths, an OpenAPI document, or a WebSocket handshake.
Establish whether any authentication is required, and if a token is used, where it is stored and who can read it.
Inspect the cross-origin response headers to see which origins the listener accepts.
Identify which functions the API exposes, prioritising file access, credential retrieval, update triggers and process launching.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers interacting with local listeners on the test workstation.
Enumerate ports, then request a likely root path and record the response to establish that a service is present.
Map the available endpoints from any discovery document, client-side code, or observed traffic between the application's components.
Call an unauthenticated endpoint directly and confirm it acts, not merely that it responds.
Build a local web page that issues the same request cross-origin and confirm whether the browser permits it.
Where a token is required, locate its storage and record the file permissions rather than the token value.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate listeners
examplePayloads.command: ss -ltnp | grep -i myapp    # or: netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING

examplePayloads.label: Probe the service
Discovery document
Cross-origin header check
Cross-origin reachability page
Token storage permissions

variants: A WebSocket endpoint, which is not subject to the same-origin policy at all and must validate the Origin header itself.
A listener bound to all interfaces rather than loopback, making it reachable from the local network.
DNS rebinding against a loopback listener, which defeats origin checks that rely on the hostname.
A companion browser extension whose native messaging host exposes the same functions without any network listener.
mitigation: Bind to loopback only, and verify this rather than assuming the default.
Require authentication on every endpoint using a token generated per session and stored with permissions readable only by the owning user.
Validate the Origin header explicitly against an allowlist, and apply this to WebSocket upgrades as well as HTTP requests.
Require a custom header on every request so that simple cross-origin requests cannot reach the API without a preflight.
Keep privileged functions such as file access, update triggers and credential retrieval off the local API entirely.
Prefer a named pipe or Unix domain socket with operating-system access control over an HTTP listener where the communication is genuinely local.

items.title: Insecure OAuth and SSO Token Handling in Desktop Clients
items.prerequisites: A desktop application that authenticates through a browser-based OAuth or single sign-on flow and caches the resulting tokens locally. A test account and a workstation where the application can be authenticated. The ability to inspect local storage locations and to intercept the loopback callback, and authorisation covering handling of tokens issued to the test account.
items.whatItIs: Desktop clients authenticate by opening a browser, receiving a callback on a loopback address, and caching the resulting refresh token so the user is not prompted again. Each of those steps has a specific failure mode: the loopback callback can be raced or claimed by another local process, and the cached refresh token is a long-lived credential that frequently sits in a plain file. A stolen refresh token is often more valuable than a password, since it already represents a completed multi-factor authentication.
items.rootCause: The loopback redirect is chosen because it needs no registered custom scheme, but any local process can bind a port or register a competing handler. Token caches are written with the platform's default file permissions rather than the platform's credential store, because the credential store is more work and the file approach is portable. Refresh tokens are issued with long lifetimes for user convenience, and clients rarely bind them to the device.
items.impact: A recovered refresh token grants continuing access to the account without a password and without triggering multi-factor authentication, since the factor was satisfied when the token was issued. It typically survives a password change, so the usual containment step does not revoke it. Any local process running as the user can read a file-based cache, which means a low-privilege compromise or a shared workstation is enough. Where the token covers a cloud productivity suite, the reach extends well beyond the desktop application.
stepsToIdentify: Trace the authentication flow and record whether it uses a loopback redirect, a custom scheme, or an embedded browser.
Confirm whether PKCE is used, and whether the state parameter is validated on return.

Establish refresh token lifetime and whether it is bound to the device or usable from anywhere.
Check whether an embedded browser is used, since that lets the application observe credentials directly.

Authenticate normally and capture the callback request to the loopback address, noting the port and whether it is fixed.
Locate the resulting token cache and record its permissions before opening it.
Determine whether the cached token can be read as another process running under the same user.

items.title: Installer and Repair-Mode Privilege Escalation
items.prerequisites: An application distributed through a platform installer package that supports repair or modify operations. A workstation with the application installed and a standard, non-administrative user account. Authorisation to attempt local privilege escalation, and a snapshot or restore point since repair operations modify the installed state.
items.whatItIs: Installers run with elevated privileges, and many platforms allow a standard user to trigger repair without prompting so that a broken installation can be fixed without an administrator. Repair re-executes installer actions as the system account, including custom actions written by the vendor. If any of those actions touches a path the user can write, or launches a helper the user can replace, the user controls code running with full privileges.
items.rootCause: Custom installer actions are written to work during a first installation, where the environment is assumed to be clean and the user is assumed to be an administrator. Repair reuses those same actions in a context where neither assumption holds. Temporary directories, user-writable installation paths and unquoted service paths all become exploitable once the action runs elevated on demand. The elevation is by design; the attacker simply supplies the input.
items.impact: A standard user obtains full system privileges on the endpoint, which defeats the separation the organisation relies on for endpoint management. It is reliable and repeatable because it depends on installed software rather than on a timing condition, and it is widely applicable wherever that software is deployed. Escalation of this kind is also a common step after an initial foothold, turning a limited compromise into complete control of the machine.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the installer technology and whether repair or modify can be initiated by a standard user without prompting.
Enumerate custom actions in the installer package and note which run with elevated privileges.
Check the permissions on the installation directory and on any directory the installer writes to during repair.
Look for unquoted service paths and for services whose binary sits in a user-writable location.
Observe a repair operation and record every file and registry write, noting any path under user control.
Determine whether the installer validates the signature of files it executes or copies during repair.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers local privilege escalation and take a restore point before modifying anything.
Trigger a repair as a standard user and confirm it completes without an administrative prompt.
Monitor file system and registry activity during repair, filtering for writes and executions in user-writable paths.
Identify a specific operation where a path the user controls is read or executed by the elevated process.
Place a benign marker at that path — a file write or a process launch recorded to a log — rather than a payload.
Re-run the repair and confirm the marker executed with system privileges, then restore the original state.

variants: Advertised shortcut repair, which triggers the same elevated path when a user launches a shortcut with a missing component.
An auto-updater running as a service that fetches or executes from a user-writable staging directory.
Rollback abuse, where the restore path is writable and the rollback executes files the user placed there.
A DLL search order weakness in the installer process itself, exploitable because the process runs elevated.
mitigation: Restrict repair and modify operations to administrators where the platform allows it.
Ensure the installation directory and every staging directory used during repair are writable only by administrators.
Quote all service paths and place service binaries outside user-writable locations.
Validate the signature of any file the installer executes or copies during repair, and fail closed when validation fails.
Use absolute paths and a controlled search order for any library or helper an elevated installer action loads.
Include the repair path in security testing of the installer, since it is routinely tested only on first installation.
