items.title: Unsigned or Unvalidated Plugin and Add-In Loading
items.prerequisites: An application with an extension mechanism: plugins, add-ins, scripts, themes or language packs. A workstation with the application installed and write access to a location the application searches for extensions. Authorisation to load a tester-authored extension, and agreement that it will do nothing beyond recording that it executed.
items.whatItIs: An extension mechanism is a deliberate code execution path into the application's process, and it is often the least protected one. Many applications load anything found in a plugin directory, with no signature check and no record of what was loaded. Because the extension runs inside the application, it inherits whatever privileges and trust the application holds — stored credentials, open sessions, network access through the application's own permitted paths.
items.rootCause: Extension mechanisms are designed for flexibility, and signature enforcement adds friction for the developers who write extensions, so it is frequently omitted or made optional. The plugin directory is often placed under the user profile so extensions can be installed without administrator rights, which also means any process running as the user can write there. Loading typically happens at startup with no user-visible record of what was loaded.
items.impact: Code placed in the plugin directory runs inside a trusted application, which is both a persistence mechanism and a privilege inheritance. If the application runs elevated or holds cached credentials, the extension has them too. Endpoint protection frequently permits the behaviour because the activity is attributed to a known application. Where extensions are distributed through a marketplace, a single compromised extension reaches every organisation that installed it.
stepsToIdentify: Identify every location the application searches for extensions, including user-profile paths and any configurable search path.
Check the file system permissions on each location to determine who can add files there.
Determine whether extensions are signature-checked before loading, and whether an invalid signature blocks or merely warns.
Establish what privileges an extension inherits: process privileges, stored credentials, and network access.
Review whether the application records which extensions were loaded, and whether that record is available to endpoint monitoring.
Assess how extensions are distributed and whether the organisation controls which ones may be installed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers loading a tester-authored extension and agree it will only record its own execution context.
Write a minimal extension conforming to the documented interface that logs the process identity and privileges it runs under.
Place it in the search path as a standard user and restart the application.
Confirm from the log that it executed inside the application process.
Test signature enforcement by modifying the extension after signing, or by omitting a signature entirely, and record the behaviour.
Determine what the extension could reach — stored credentials, configuration, session state — by enumerating availability rather than by extracting anything.

variants: A configurable search path that can be redirected through an environment variable or configuration setting.
Marketplace distribution where a legitimate extension is updated maliciously after gaining an install base.
Script-based extensions interpreted at runtime, which evade file-based detection more easily than compiled ones.
Theme or language packs that are treated as data but are processed by a parser capable of executing code.
mitigation: Require valid signatures on all extensions and fail closed, refusing to load anything that does not validate.
Place extension directories outside user-writable paths, or require elevation to install an extension.
Maintain an organisation-level allowlist of permitted extensions where the application supports policy control.
Log every extension load with its identity and signature status, and make that log available to endpoint monitoring.
Run extensions with reduced privileges where the platform supports it, rather than granting full process trust.
Prompt the user when a new extension appears, since silent loading removes the only remaining chance to notice.

items.title: Telemetry and Third-Party SDK Data Exfiltration
items.prerequisites: A desktop application that reports telemetry, crash data or analytics, which covers most commercial software. A workstation with the application installed and an intercepting proxy with a trusted root certificate. Authorisation to intercept application traffic, and awareness that captured telemetry may contain real user data requiring careful handling.
items.whatItIs: Telemetry is disclosed in general terms — usage data, diagnostics — but what is actually transmitted is rarely examined. Crash reports in particular tend to include memory contents, which can contain whatever the application was processing: documents, credentials, customer records. Third-party analytics and crash SDKs send to the vendor's own endpoints rather than the application vendor's, so data leaves for destinations the organisation never assessed.
items.rootCause: Telemetry is added by developers to diagnose problems, and more data makes diagnosis easier, so the default tends toward collecting broadly. Crash handlers capture memory because that is what makes a crash debuggable, and redaction is difficult to do well. Third-party SDKs are integrated for convenience and their network behaviour is rarely reviewed. Opt-out settings frequently govern only some of the collection paths, with crash reporting often exempt.
items.impact: Sensitive data leaves the organisation to a third party that was never assessed and may be in a different jurisdiction, which is a regulatory problem independent of any attacker. For applications handling regulated data, a crash report containing record contents is a disclosure. The traffic also creates an egress path that appears legitimate to monitoring, and a compromised analytics SDK would deliver a supply chain compromise directly into the application process.
stepsToIdentify: Intercept application traffic over an extended session and enumerate every distinct destination, separating vendor endpoints from third parties.
Identify which third-party SDKs are present, from the binary's imports, bundled libraries or observed endpoints.
Capture and examine the content of telemetry payloads rather than accepting the documented description.
Trigger a crash deliberately and inspect the crash report for memory contents, file paths, user names and any document data.
Test whether the opt-out setting actually stops transmission, and whether it covers crash reporting as well as analytics.
Determine whether telemetry is sent over pinned or validated TLS, since an unvalidated channel is also an injection path.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers traffic interception and agree how any captured user data will be handled and destroyed.
Configure the proxy with a trusted root and confirm the application's traffic is visible.
Use the application normally with distinctive marker data so any transmission of it is identifiable.
Enumerate destinations and payload contents, recording which markers appear in outbound traffic.
Trigger a crash while the marker data is in memory and examine the resulting report for its presence.
Disable telemetry through the application's own setting, repeat, and record precisely what still transmits.

Validate TLS strictly on telemetry endpoints, since the channel is also a path into the application.
Provide an enterprise policy to disable telemetry centrally, since individual opt-out does not scale to a managed estate.

items.title: Multi-User and Shared Workstation Data Exposure
items.prerequisites: A desktop application installed on a workstation used by more than one account: shared terminals, kiosks, clinical workstations, trading floors, or any machine with roaming profiles. Two test accounts on the same machine, neither with administrative rights. Authorisation to read files belonging to another account where permissions allow it.
items.whatItIs: Applications are usually built and tested on a developer's own machine, where they are the only user, so data placed in shared locations causes no visible problem. On a shared workstation the same behaviour exposes one user's data to another. The common cases are caches and temporary files written to a world-readable shared directory, a database in the installation directory used by every account, and cached credentials or session tokens that persist after the first user logs out.
items.rootCause: Writing to a shared location is often the path of least resistance during development, particularly for caches and logs where a per-user path requires more work. Installation directories are sometimes made writable to allow updates without elevation, which simultaneously makes application data readable to everyone. Cleanup on logout is rarely implemented because the single-user assumption means there is nothing to clean up from another user's perspective.
items.impact: One user of a shared workstation can read another's documents, cached records, session state or credentials without any privilege escalation, using ordinary file access. In clinical, financial or call-centre environments this crosses a real confidentiality boundary and is usually a reportable event rather than only a technical weakness. Because it needs no exploitation, it will not appear in any monitoring, and it may have been occurring since installation.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every location the application writes to during normal use, including temporary and cache directories.
Record the permissions on each path and identify which are readable or writable by other local accounts.
Check whether the application database or configuration sits in the installation directory rather than under a user profile.
Log in as a second account and attempt to read the first account's application data directly.
Determine whether cached credentials, tokens or session state persist after the first user logs out.
Where roaming profiles are used, establish whether application data is synchronised and where the copy is stored.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers accessing data belonging to another test account on the shared workstation.
As the first account, use the application so that it caches identifiable marker data.
Record every file the application created or modified, along with its permissions.
Log out, log in as the second account, and attempt to read each of those paths.
Record specifically what was readable and whether the marker data was recoverable in plaintext.
Check whether the second account can also modify the first account's data, since write access permits tampering rather than only disclosure.

variants: A kiosk or clinical workstation with a shared generic account, where every user's data accumulates under one profile.
Roaming profiles synchronising application data to a file server where it is exposed more broadly.
Temporary files written to a shared temporary directory and never deleted after the session ends.
A shared local database used by all accounts with no per-user access control inside it.
mitigation: Write all application data under the per-user profile with permissions restricted to that user.
Keep the installation directory read-only for standard users, and never place mutable application data there.
Clear caches, tokens and temporary files at logout, and verify by inspecting the disk rather than by assuming.
Where a shared database is genuinely required, enforce per-user access control within it and encrypt per-user content with a user-bound key.
Exclude sensitive application data from roaming profile synchronisation.
Test the application explicitly in a multi-account configuration, since single-user testing cannot surface this class of issue.
